clip.title: How np.clip() works
clip.description: Limits every value in an array to a minimum and a maximum.

slides.caption: np.clip() gets the array [1, 5, 9, 12] and the limits 3 and 10.
Each value is checked. 1 is below the minimum 3 and 12 is above the maximum 10 (red). 5 and 9 are inside the range (green).
Values outside the range are replaced by the nearest limit: 1 becomes 3 and 12 becomes 10. Values inside stay the same.

argsort.title: How np.argsort() works
argsort.description: Gives the positions that would sort an array.

note.text: returns the positions (indexes), not the values

slides.caption: np.argsort() gets [30, 10, 20]. Each value sits at an index: 30 at 0, 10 at 1, 20 at 2.
The smallest value is 10 and it sits at index 1, so the result starts with 1.
The next smallest is 20, at index 2.
The largest is 30, at index 0.
np.argsort([30, 10, 20]) = [1, 2, 0]. Reading the original array in this order gives it sorted: 10, 20, 30.

cumsum.title: How np.cumsum() works
cumsum.description: Gives the running total of the values in an array.

slides.caption: np.cumsum() gets [1, 2, 3, 4] and adds the values up as it goes.
The first result is just the first value: 1.
Add the next value to the total so far: 1 + 2 = 3.
Again: 3 + 3 = 6.
And again: 6 + 4 = 10.

reshape.title: How np.reshape() works
reshape.description: Arranges the same values into a new shape.

slides.caption: np.reshape() gets six numbers in a row and the new shape (2, 3): 2 rows and 3 columns.
It fills the first row from the start of the data: 0, 1, 2.
Then it fills the second row with the next values: 3, 4, 5. The values are not changed, only how they are arranged.

sum.title: How np.sum() works
sum.description: Adds up all the values in an array.

slides.caption: np.sum() gets the array [1, 2, 3, 4] and adds all its values.
Start with the first value: the total is 1.
Add the next value: 1 + 2 = 3.
Add the next value: 3 + 3 = 6.
Add the last value: 6 + 4 = 10.
np.sum([1, 2, 3, 4]) = 10 (one number for the whole array)

mean.title: How np.mean() works
mean.description: Gives the average of the values in an array.

note.text: sum divided by how many values

slides.caption: np.mean() gets the array [2, 4, 6, 8].
First it adds up all the values: 2 + 4 + 6 + 8 = 20.
Then it divides by how many values there are (4): 20 / 4 = 5.0.

max.title: How np.max() works
max.description: Finds the largest value in an array.

note.text: keep the biggest value seen so far

slides.caption: np.max() gets the array [3, 9, 2, 7] and looks for the largest value.
The first value, 3, is the biggest so far.
9 is bigger than 3, so 9 is the new biggest.
2 is smaller than 9, so 9 stays.
7 is smaller than 9 too.

argmax.title: How np.argmax() works
argmax.description: Gives the position of the largest value in an array.

note.text: returns the position, not the value

slides.caption: np.argmax() gets [3, 9, 2, 7]. It returns the INDEX of the largest value.
The first value, 3, is the biggest so far, at index 0.
9 is bigger than 3, so the best index becomes 1.
2 is smaller than 9, so the best index stays 1.
7 is smaller than 9 as well.
np.argmax([3, 9, 2, 7]) = 1 (the 9 sits at index 1)

sort.title: How np.sort() works
sort.description: Returns a sorted copy of an array, smallest first.

note.text: returns a sorted COPY, the original is unchanged

slides.caption: np.sort() gets [4, 1, 3, 2].
The smallest value is 1, so it goes first.
The next smallest is 2.
Then 3.
And the largest, 4, goes last.
np.sort([4, 1, 3, 2]) = [1, 2, 3, 4]. The input array is not changed.

flip.title: How np.flip() works
flip.description: Reverses the order of the values in an array.

slides.caption: np.flip() gets [1, 2, 3, 4].
The last value, 4, becomes the first.
The second-to-last value, 3, becomes the second.
Then 2.
And the first value, 1, ends up last.

repeat.title: How np.repeat() works
repeat.description: Repeats each value of an array a number of times.

note.text: each VALUE is repeated 2 times in a row

slides.caption: np.repeat() gets [1, 2, 3] and the number 2.
The first value, 1, is written 2 times: 1, 1.
Then 2 is written 2 times.
Then 3 is written 2 times.

tile.title: How np.tile() works
tile.description: Repeats a whole array again and again.

note.text: the WHOLE array is repeated 2 times

slides.caption: np.tile() gets [1, 2, 3] and the number 2.
The whole array is written once: 1, 2, 3.
Then the whole array is written a second time.
np.tile([1, 2, 3], 2) = [1, 2, 3, 1, 2, 3]. Compare np.repeat, which repeats each value.

diff.title: How np.diff() works
diff.description: Gives the differences between neighbouring values.

note.text: each value minus the one before it

slides.caption: np.diff() gets [1, 4, 9, 16]. The result has one item fewer.
First pair: 4 - 1 = 3.
Next pair: 9 - 4 = 5.
Last pair: 16 - 9 = 7.

unique.title: How np.unique() works
unique.description: Gives the sorted distinct values of an array.

slides.caption: np.unique() gets [3, 1, 2, 3, 1]. Some values appear more than once.
The smallest distinct value is 1. It appears at index 1 and 4, but is kept only once.
Next comes 2 (it appears once).
Then 3, which appears at index 0 and 3, kept once.
np.concatenate() gets two arrays: [1, 2, 3] (blue) and [4, 5, 6] (second colour).
The values of the first array come first.
The values of the second array follow directly after them.

transpose.title: How np.transpose() works
transpose.description: Swaps the rows and columns of an array.

slides.caption: np.transpose() gets a 2 × 3 array: 2 rows and 3 columns.
The first ROW (1, 2, 3) becomes the first COLUMN.
The second row (4, 5, 6) becomes the second column.

stack.title: How np.stack() works
stack.description: Joins arrays along a NEW axis.

note.text: two arrays of shape (3,)  →  one of shape (2, 3)

slides.caption: np.stack() gets two arrays that have the same shape: [1, 2, 3] and [4, 5, 6].
The first array becomes row 0 of a new, taller array.
The second array becomes row 1. stack() adds a new axis, so the result has one more dimension.

ones.title: How np.ones() works
ones.description: Makes a new array filled with ones.

slides.caption: np.ones() gets a shape: (2, 3) means 2 rows and 3 columns.
It makes a new array with that shape: 2 × 3 = 6 cells.
Every cell is set to 1. The default type is float, so the values print as 1.0.

eye.title: How np.eye() works
eye.description: Makes an identity-style matrix: ones on the diagonal, zeros elsewhere.

slides.caption: np.eye() gets N = 3, so it makes a square 3 × 3 matrix.
A new array with 3 rows and 3 columns is made.
All cells start as 0.0.
The diagonal (row 0 col 0, row 1 col 1, row 2 col 2) is set to 1.0.

linspace.title: How np.linspace() works
linspace.description: Makes evenly spaced numbers between a start and a stop.

slides.caption: np.linspace() gets a start of 0, a stop of 1 and num = 5: it must make 5 evenly spaced numbers from 0 to 1.
The first number is the start (0.0) and the last is the stop (1.0).
5 points make 4 gaps, so each step is (1 - 0) / 4 = 0.25.
Stepping 0.25 at a time from the start fills in the points between: 0.25, 0.5 and 0.75.

dot.title: How np.dot() works
dot.description: Multiplies matching items and adds them up (the dot product).

slides.caption: np.dot() gets two 1-D arrays of the same length: [1, 2, 3] and [4, 5, 6].
Items in the same position are multiplied: 1 × 4 = 4, 2 × 5 = 10 and 3 × 6 = 18.
The products are added up: 4 + 10 + 18 = 32.
np.dot([1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]) = 32 (the dot product, a single number)

where.title: How np.where() works
where.description: Picks values from x or y depending on a condition.

note.text: pick from x where True, from y where False

slides.caption: cond = [True, False, True, False], x = [1, 2, 3, 4], y = [10, 20, 30, 40]. np.where() works column by column.
Where cond is True the result takes the value from x: 1 in column 0 and 3 in column 2.
Where cond is False it takes the value from y instead: 20 in column 1 and 40 in column 3.
np.where(cond, x, y) = [1, 20, 3, 40]

argmin.title: How np.argmin() works
argmin.description: Gives the position of the smallest value in an array.

note.text: returns the position, not the value

slides.caption: np.argmin() gets [3, 9, 2, 7]. It returns the INDEX of the smallest value.
The first value, 3, is the smallest so far, at index 0.
9 is not smaller than 3, so the best index stays 0.
2 is smaller than 3, so the best index becomes 2.
7 is not smaller than 2.
np.argmin([3, 9, 2, 7]) = 2 (the 2 sits at index 2)

min.title: How np.min() works
min.description: Finds the smallest value, either in the whole array or along an axis.

slides.caption: np.min() gets a 2 × 2 array. With axis=0 it works on each column separately.
Column 0 holds 3 and 2. The smaller one is 2.
Column 1 holds 9 and 7. The smaller one is 7.
np.min([[3, 9], [2, 7]], axis=0) = [2, 7]. Without axis it would return the one smallest value of everything: 2.

prod.title: How np.prod() works
prod.description: Multiplies all the values in an array.

slides.caption: np.prod() gets [1, 2, 3, 4] and multiplies all its values.
Start with the first value: 1.

cumprod.title: How np.cumprod() works
cumprod.description: Gives the running product of the values in an array.

slides.caption: np.cumprod() gets [1, 2, 3, 4]. Every result is the product of all values so far.
The first result is just the first value: 1.

any.title: How np.any() works
any.description: Tells whether at least one value is true (non-zero).

note.text: True if at least one value is non-zero

slides.caption: np.any() gets [0, 0, 3, 0]. Zero counts as False, every other number counts as True.
0 is False.
0 is False.
3 is True. One true value is enough to make the answer True.
The last 0 does not change the answer.
np.any([0, 0, 3, 0]) = True

all.title: How np.all() works
all.description: Tells whether every value is true (non-zero).

note.text: True only if every value is non-zero

slides.caption: np.all() gets [1, 2, 0, 4]. Zero counts as False, every other number counts as True.
1 is True.
2 is True.
0 is False. One false value is enough to make the answer False.
The last value, 4, cannot fix it.
np.all([1, 2, 0, 4]) = False

var.title: How np.var() works
var.description: Measures how spread out the values are (the variance).

note.text: average squared distance from the mean

slides.caption: np.var() gets 8 values.
Then it squares each value's distance from 5: 9, 1, 1, 1, 0, 0, 4, 16. These add up to 32.
The variance is their average: 32 / 8 = 4.0.

std.title: How np.std() works
std.description: Measures how spread out the values are (the standard deviation).

slides.caption: np.std() gets 8 values.
The variance is the average squared distance from the mean: 32 / 8 = 4.0.
The standard deviation is the square root of the variance: √4.0 = 2.0.

median.title: How np.median() works
median.description: Finds the middle value of an array.

slides.caption: np.median() gets [7, 1, 5, 3, 9].
Sorted, the values are 1, 3, 5, 7, 9.
There are 5 values, so the middle one is the 3rd: 5. The result is a float: 5.0.

average.title: How np.average() works
average.description: Gives the average, optionally giving some values more weight.

slides.caption: np.average() gets [1, 2, 3, 4] and the weights [4, 3, 2, 1]: earlier values count more.
Multiply each value by its weight and add: 1×4 + 2×3 + 3×2 + 4×1 = 20.
Divide by the sum of the weights: 20 / (4+3+2+1) = 20 / 10 = 2.0.

round.title: How np.round() works
round.description: Rounds numbers to a given number of decimals.

slides.caption: np.round() gets [1.26, 2.44, 3.78] and decimals = 1: keep one digit after the point.
1.26: the second decimal is 6, so it rounds up to 1.3.
2.44: the second decimal is 4, so it rounds down to 2.4.
3.78: the second decimal is 8, so it rounds up to 3.8.

count-nonzero.title: How np.count_nonzero() works
count-nonzero.description: Counts the values that are not zero.

note.text: how many values are not zero

slides.caption: np.count_nonzero() gets [0, 1, 0, 2, 3].
0 is zero: not counted. The count is 0.
1 is not zero: count = 1.
0: not counted.
2 is not zero: count = 2.
3 is not zero: count = 3.
np.count_nonzero([0, 1, 0, 2, 3]) = 3

nonzero.title: How np.nonzero() works
nonzero.description: Gives the positions of the values that are not zero.

note.text: returns positions (a tuple holding one array)

slides.caption: np.nonzero() gets [0, 1, 0, 2, 3] and finds where the values are not zero.
1 at index 1 is not zero, so index 1 is kept.
2 at index 3 is not zero: index 3.
3 at index 4 is not zero: index 4.
np.nonzero([0, 1, 0, 2, 3]) = (array([1, 3, 4]),). It is a tuple with one array per dimension.

searchsorted.title: How np.searchsorted() works
searchsorted.description: Finds where a value would fit in a sorted array.

note.text: the array must already be sorted

slides.caption: np.searchsorted() gets the sorted array [1, 3, 5, 7] and the value 4.
1 and 3 are both smaller than 4, so 4 must go after them.
5 is not smaller than 4, so 4 goes just before it: at index 2.
np.searchsorted([1, 3, 5, 7], 4) = 2: inserting 4 at index 2 keeps the array sorted.

take.title: How np.take() works
take.description: Picks values from an array by their index.

slides.caption: np.take() gets [10, 20, 30, 40] and the indices [3, 0].
The first index is 3, so it takes the value at index 3: 40.
The next index is 0: the value 10.

roll.title: How np.roll() works
roll.description: Shifts values along an array; those pushed off one end wrap around.

slides.caption: np.roll() gets [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] and a shift of 2.
Everything moves 2 places to the right. The last two values, 4 and 5, fall off the end and wrap around to the front.
The other values shift right by 2: 1, 2, 3.

compress.title: How np.compress() works
compress.description: Keeps the values where a condition is true.

slides.caption: np.compress() gets the condition [True, False, True, False] and the array [1, 2, 3, 4]. The colours show the condition.
The condition for 1 is True, so 1 is kept.
The condition for 2 is False, so 2 is dropped.
True for 3: kept.
False for 4: dropped.
np.compress([True, False, True, False], [1, 2, 3, 4]) = [1, 3]. This is the same idea as boolean-mask indexing.

append.title: How np.append() works
append.description: Adds values to the end of an array, giving a new array.

slides.caption: np.append() gets the array [1, 2, 3] and the values [4, 5] to add.
The original values are copied first.
The new values follow at the end. The original array is not changed.

insert.title: How np.insert() works
insert.description: Puts a value into an array at a given index, giving a new array.

slides.caption: np.insert() gets [1, 2, 3], the index 1 and the value 99.
Values before index 1 stay where they are: 1.
The new value 99 goes in at index 1.
The values from index 1 on move one place to the right.

delete.title: How np.delete() works
delete.description: Removes the value at a given index, giving a new array.

slides.caption: np.delete() gets [1, 2, 3, 4] and the index 1.
The value at index 0 is kept.
The value at index 1 (the 2) is left out.
The rest is kept and closes the gap.

vstack.title: How np.vstack() works
vstack.description: Stacks arrays on top of each other, as rows.

note.text: vertical stack: one array per row

slides.caption: np.vstack() gets two 1-D arrays of the same length: [1, 2, 3] and [4, 5, 6].
The first array becomes the top row.
The second array becomes the row below it.
np.hstack() gets two 1-D arrays: [1, 2, 3] and [4, 5, 6].
The first array comes first.
The second array is placed right after it. For 1-D arrays this is the same as concatenate.

split.title: How np.split() works
split.description: Cuts an array into equal parts.

slides.caption: np.split() gets [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6] and 3. It must cut the array into 3 equal parts, so each part has 2 items.
It takes the first 2 items and puts them in a new group: [1, 2].
It moves on 2 positions and takes the next 2 items: [3, 4].
It moves on 2 positions and takes the next 2 items: [5, 6].

array-split.title: How np.array_split() works
array-split.description: Cuts an array into parts, even when it does not divide evenly.

slides.caption: np.array_split() gets [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] and 3. 5 items cannot be cut into 3 equal parts, so the first parts get one extra item: sizes 2, 2, 1.
It takes the first 2 items and puts them in a new group: [1, 2].
It moves on 2 positions and takes the next 2 items: [3, 4].
Only 1 item is left, so the last group is shorter: [5]. Then the end is reached.

full.title: How np.full() works
full.description: Makes a new array filled with one value.

slides.caption: np.full() gets a shape (2, 2) and a fill value 7.
It makes a new array with 2 rows and 2 columns: 4 cells.
Every cell is set to 7.

zeros-like.title: How np.zeros_like() works
zeros-like.description: Makes an array of zeros with the same shape as another array.

note.text: same shape and type as the input

slides.caption: np.zeros_like() gets [[1, 2], [3, 4]]. It only looks at its shape (2, 2) and type (integers).
A new array with the same shape, 2 rows and 2 columns, is made.
Every cell is set to 0. The values of the input are not used.
np.identity() gets n = 3, so it makes a square 3 × 3 matrix.
A new array with 3 rows and 3 columns is made.
All cells start as 0.0.
The diagonal is set to 1.0.

diag.title: How np.diag() works
diag.description: Makes a diagonal matrix from a list, or reads the diagonal of a matrix.

slides.caption: np.diag() gets the 1-D array [1, 2, 3]. A 1-D input is placed on the diagonal of a square matrix.
A 3 × 3 matrix is made, one row and column per input value.
All cells start as 0.
The input values go on the diagonal: 1, 2, 3.

outer.title: How np.outer() works
outer.description: Multiplies every value of one array with every value of another.

note.text: every pair: row value × column value

slides.caption: np.outer() gets [1, 2, 3] and [10, 20]. The result has one row per value of the first and one column per value of the second.
A 3 × 2 table is made: 3 values × 2 values.

trace.title: How np.trace() works
trace.description: Adds up the diagonal of a matrix.

slides.caption: np.trace() gets the 2 × 2 matrix [[1, 2], [3, 4]].
The main diagonal runs from the top left to the bottom right: 1 and 4.
It adds them: 1 + 4 = 5.

triu.title: How np.triu() works
triu.description: Keeps the upper triangle of a matrix and zeros the rest.

slides.caption: np.triu() gets a 3 × 3 matrix.
The diagonal and everything above it is kept.
The cells below the diagonal are set to 0.

tril.title: How np.tril() works
tril.description: Keeps the lower triangle of a matrix and zeros the rest.

slides.caption: np.tril() gets a 3 × 3 matrix.
The diagonal and everything below it is kept.
The cells above the diagonal are set to 0.

fliplr.title: How np.fliplr() works
fliplr.description: Mirrors a matrix left to right.

slides.caption: np.fliplr() gets a 2 × 3 matrix. "lr" means left-right.
Row 0 is reversed: 1, 2, 3 becomes 3, 2, 1.
Row 1 is reversed too: 4, 5, 6 becomes 6, 5, 4.

note.text: reverses the order of the rows

slides.caption: np.flipud() gets a 2 × 3 matrix. "ud" means up-down.
The rows swap places: the top row 1, 2, 3 moves to the bottom and the bottom row 4, 5, 6 moves to the top.
Inside each row the order stays the same. Only the order of the rows is reversed.
np.rot90() gets [[1, 2], [3, 4]] and turns it a quarter turn counter-clockwise.
The top row (1, 2) becomes the left column, with 1 at the bottom and 2 at the top. The bottom row (3, 4) becomes the right column, with 3 at the bottom and 4 at the top.
In total, every value moved one quarter turn counter-clockwise around the centre.

ravel.title: How np.ravel() works
ravel.description: Flattens an array into one dimension.

slides.caption: np.ravel() gets a 2 × 3 array.
It reads the first row from left to right: 1, 2, 3.
Then the second row: 4, 5, 6. All values end up in one line.

isin.title: How np.isin() works
isin.description: Tests which values of an array appear in another array.

slides.caption: np.isin() checks every value of [1, 2, 3, 4] against the test values [2, 4].
1 is not in [2, 4]: False.
2 is in [2, 4]: True.
3 is not in [2, 4]: False.
4 is in [2, 4]: True.
np.isin([1, 2, 3, 4], [2, 4]) = [False, True, False, True]

intersect1d.title: How np.intersect1d() works
intersect1d.description: Finds the values that appear in both arrays.

slides.caption: np.intersect1d() gets [1, 2, 3, 4] (first colour) and [3, 4, 5] (second colour).
3 appears in both arrays, so it is in the result.
4 appears in both arrays too. 1, 2 and 5 appear in only one.

union1d.title: How np.union1d() works
union1d.description: Combines two arrays into their sorted distinct values.

note.text: sorted values from either, once each

slides.caption: np.union1d() gets [1, 2, 3] (first colour) and [3, 4] (second colour).
1 is in the result.
2 is in the result.
3 is in both arrays but is kept only once.
4 is in the result.

setdiff1d.title: How np.setdiff1d() works
setdiff1d.description: Finds the values of one array that are not in another.

note.text: in the first array but not in the second

slides.caption: np.setdiff1d() gets [1, 2, 3, 4] (first colour) and [2, 4] (second colour).
1 is not in [2, 4], so it is kept.
2 is in [2, 4], so it is dropped.
3 is not in [2, 4], so it is kept.
4 is in [2, 4], so it is dropped.

copy.title: How np.copy() works
copy.description: Makes an independent copy of an array.

slides.caption: a is the array [1, 2, 3]. np.copy(a) will make a separate array b.
np.copy() allocates new memory and copies the values: b is [1, 2, 3]. b and a are now independent.
Now we set b[0] = 99. Only the copy changes.
After b[0] = 99: b = [99, 2, 3], but a is still [1, 2, 3]. A copy never changes the original (unlike a view).

broadcast-to.title: How np.broadcast_to() works
broadcast-to.description: Stretches an array to a bigger shape without copying data.

slides.caption: np.broadcast_to() gets the 1-D array [1, 2, 3] (shape (3,)) and the target shape (2, 3): 2 rows of 3.
Row 0 of the result is the array itself: 1, 2, 3.
The array is stretched along the new axis: row 1 shows the same 1, 2, 3 again.
No data is copied: the result is a read-only view that reuses the same 3 values for every row. This stretching is called broadcasting.

broadcast-arrays.title: How np.broadcast_arrays() works
broadcast-arrays.description: Stretches arrays of different shapes to one common shape.

slides.caption: The first array is a column [[1], [2]] (shape (2, 1)). The second is a row [10, 20, 30] (shape (3,)). Their shapes differ.
The first array is stretched sideways: its single column is repeated to make 3 columns.
The second array is stretched downwards: its row is repeated to make 2 rows.
Both arrays now have the same shape (2, 3). Operations like a + b use this same stretching.

ndarray.title: How the NumPy array (ndarray) works
ndarray.description: The NumPy array: a grid of values of one type, with a shape.

note.text: an ndarray: a grid of values that all have the same type

slides.caption: np.array() builds an ndarray from nested lists: here 2 rows and 3 columns of numbers.
shape is the length along each axis: 2 rows and 3 columns, so (2, 3).
ndim is the number of axes: 2 (rows and columns).
size is the total number of values: 2 × 3 = 6.
dtype is the one type shared by all values. Whole numbers give an integer type, usually int64.

dtype.title: How the NumPy data type (dtype) works
dtype.description: Every NumPy array has one data type, and you can convert between types.

note.text: dtype: the type shared by all values

slides.caption: np.array([1, 2, 3]) holds whole numbers, so its dtype is an integer type, usually int64.
.astype(float) makes a new array in which every value is converted to a floating-point number.
NumPy also picks a dtype for you: np.array([1, 2.5]) becomes float64, because one value has a decimal part and all values must share one type.
A dtype fixes how much memory each value uses and how it behaves. np.array([1, 2, 3]).astype(float) = [1.0, 2.0, 3.0] (float64).

swapaxes.title: How np.swapaxes() works
swapaxes.description: Swaps two axes of an array.

slides.caption: np.swapaxes() gets a 2 × 3 array and the axes 0 and 1 to swap.
The first ROW (1, 2, 3) becomes the first COLUMN.
The second row (4, 5, 6) becomes the second column.

einsum.title: How np.einsum() works
einsum.description: Writes sums of products over axes in a short text formula.

note.text: 'ij->ji': input axes i, j  →  output axes j, i

slides.caption: np.einsum() gets the formula 'ij->ji' and a 2 × 3 array. Letters name the axes: i = rows, j = columns.
The output is written as 'ji': j (columns) comes first. So the first row becomes the first column.
The second row becomes the second column.
np.einsum('ij->ji', ...) = [[1, 4], [2, 5], [3, 6]] (the transpose)

column-stack.title: How np.column_stack() works
column-stack.description: Stacks 1-D arrays as the columns of a 2-D array.

slides.caption: np.column_stack() gets two 1-D arrays: [1, 2, 3] and [4, 5, 6].
The first array becomes the first column.
The second array becomes the second column.
np.squeeze() gets [[1, 2, 3]]: shape (1, 3), one row holding 3 values.
The first axis has length 1: there is only one row. That axis carries no extra information.
squeeze() removes the length-1 axis. The shape becomes (3,).

expand-dims.title: How np.expand_dims() works
expand-dims.description: Adds a new axis of length 1.

slides.caption: np.expand_dims() gets [1, 2, 3] (shape (3,)) and axis 0.
A new axis of length 1 is inserted at position 0, in front of the existing axis.
The values are not changed; the array gets one more dimension. The shape becomes (1, 3).

atleast-2d.title: How np.atleast_2d() works
atleast-2d.description: Makes sure an array has at least 2 dimensions.

slides.caption: np.atleast_2d() gets [1, 2, 3]: a 1-D array of shape (3,).
It has only 1 dimension, but we need at least 2.
A 1-D array becomes one row: the shape changes from (3,) to (1, 3).
np.atleast_2d([1, 2, 3]) = [[1, 2, 3]]. An array that already has 2 or more dimensions is returned as it is.

diagonal.title: How np.diagonal() works
diagonal.description: Reads the diagonal of a matrix.

note.text: main diagonal: top left to bottom right

slides.caption: np.diagonal() gets the 2 × 2 matrix [[1, 2], [3, 4]].
The main diagonal holds the cells where the row number equals the column number: (0, 0) and (1, 1).
Their values 1 and 4 are read out into a 1-D array.

shape.title: How np.shape() works
shape.description: Gives the shape of an array.

slides.caption: np.shape() gets an array with 2 rows and 3 columns.
Axis 0 runs down the rows: there are 2 rows.
Axis 1 runs along the columns: there are 3 columns.

ndim.title: How np.ndim() works
ndim.description: Gives the number of dimensions (axes) of an array.

note.text: how many axes does the array have?

slides.caption: np.ndim() gets a table of numbers with rows and columns.
One axis runs down the rows (axis 0).
Another axis runs along the columns (axis 1).
np.ndim([[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]]) = 2: two axes. A flat list like [1, 2, 3] would give 1.

size.title: How np.size() works
size.description: Gives the total number of values in an array.

slides.caption: np.size() counts all values in the array, whatever its shape.
The first row has 3 values.
The second row has 3 values: 2 rows × 3 columns = 6.

ptp.title: How np.ptp() works
ptp.description: Gives the range of the values: the largest minus the smallest.

slides.caption: np.ptp() gets [3, 9, 2, 7].
The largest value is 9.
The smallest value is 2.
The result is the largest minus the smallest: 9 - 2 = 7.

choose.title: How np.choose() works
choose.description: Builds an array by picking from several choice arrays.

slides.caption: np.choose() gets the index array [0, 1, 0] and two choice arrays. Each index says which choice array to read from.
Index 0 at position 0: take position 0 of choice 0, which is 1.
Index 1 at position 1: take position 1 of choice 1, which is 20.
Index 0 at position 2: take position 2 of choice 0, which is 3.

resize.title: How np.resize() works
resize.description: Makes an array of a new size, repeating values to fill it.

slides.caption: np.resize() gets [1, 2, 3] and the new size 5. 3 values are not enough, so the array is repeated.
The original values come first: 1, 2, 3.
The array starts over to fill the 2 missing places: 1, 2.

allclose.title: How np.allclose() works
allclose.description: Tells whether two arrays are equal within a small tolerance.

note.text: are ALL pairs close to each other?

slides.caption: np.allclose() compares [1.0, 2.0] with [1.0, 2.5] pair by pair.
1.0 and 1.0 are equal, so this pair is close.
2.0 and 2.5 differ by 0.5. That is far more than the tiny default tolerance, so this pair is NOT close.
One pair that is not close is enough: the result is False.

isclose.title: How np.isclose() works
isclose.description: Tests, pair by pair, whether values are equal within a small tolerance.

slides.caption: np.isclose() compares [1.0, 2.0] with [1.0, 2.5] pair by pair.
1.0 and 1.0 are equal: True.
2.0 and 2.5 differ by 0.5, much more than the tiny default tolerance: False.
np.isclose([1.0, 2.0], [1.0, 2.5]) = [True, False]

array-equal.title: How np.array_equal() works
array-equal.description: Tells whether two arrays have the same shape and values.

slides.caption: np.array_equal() compares [1, 2, 3] with [1, 2, 3].
First it checks the shapes: both are (3,). They match.
Then every pair of values is compared: 1 = 1, 2 = 2, 3 = 3.
Nothing differs, so the result is True.
np.array_equal([1, 2, 3], [1, 2, 3]) = True

flatnonzero.title: How np.flatnonzero() works
flatnonzero.description: Gives the positions of non-zero values in the flattened array.

note.text: the array is flattened to [0, 1, 2, 0] first

slides.caption: np.flatnonzero() gets [[0, 1], [2, 0]]. It flattens it to one row: 0, 1, 2, 0.
1 at index 1 is not zero: index 1.
2 at index 2 is not zero: index 2.

cross.title: How np.cross() works
cross.description: Computes the cross product of two 3-D vectors.

slides.caption: np.cross() gets two 3-D vectors a = [1, 0, 0] and b = [0, 1, 0].
np.cross([1, 0, 0], [0, 1, 0]) = [0, 0, 1]: a vector at right angles to both inputs.

convolve.title: How np.convolve() works
convolve.description: Slides one sequence over another, adding up products.

note.text: result[n] = sum of a[k] × v[n - k]

slides.caption: np.convolve() gets a = [1, 2, 3] and v = [0, 1]. The result has 3 + 2 - 1 = 4 values.
np.convolve([1, 2, 3], [0, 1]) = [0, 1, 2, 3]: the input shifted by one place.

full-like.title: How np.full_like() works
full-like.description: Makes an array filled with one value, shaped like another array.

note.text: same shape as the input, filled with 9

slides.caption: np.full_like() gets [1, 2, 3] and the fill value 9. It only uses the shape (3,) of the first array.
A new array with the same shape, 3 cells, is made.
Every cell is set to 9.

ones-like.title: How np.ones_like() works
ones-like.description: Makes an array of ones with the same shape as another array.

note.text: same shape and type as the input

slides.caption: np.ones_like() gets [[1, 2], [3, 4]]. It only looks at its shape (2, 2) and type (integers).
A new array with the same shape, 2 rows and 2 columns, is made.
Every cell is set to 1.

geomspace.title: How np.geomspace() works
geomspace.description: Makes numbers spaced evenly on a multiplication scale.

slides.caption: np.geomspace() gets start 1, stop 1000 and num 4: four numbers where each is the previous one times the same factor.
The first number is the start (1.0) and the last is the stop (1000.0).
4 numbers make 3 steps. The factor is (1000 / 1) ^ (1/3) = 10.
Multiplying by 10 each time fills in the middle: 10.0 and 100.0.

logspace.title: How np.logspace() works
logspace.description: Makes numbers whose exponents are evenly spaced.

slides.caption: np.logspace() gets start exponent 0, stop exponent 3 and num 4.
First it makes 4 evenly spaced exponents from 0 to 3: 0, 1, 2, 3.
Then it raises 10 to each exponent: 10^0 = 1 and 10^1 = 10.

digitize.title: How np.digitize() works
digitize.description: Tells which bin each value falls in.

slides.caption: np.digitize() gets 4 values and the bin edges [0, 1, 2.5, 4, 10]. Bin 1 is [0, 1), bin 2 is [1, 2.5), bin 3 is [2.5, 4), bin 4 is [4, 10).
0.2 lies in [0, 1): bin 1.
6.4 lies in [4, 10): bin 4.
3.0 lies in [2.5, 4): bin 3.
1.6 lies in [1, 2.5): bin 2.

extract.title: How np.extract() works
extract.description: Picks the values where a condition is true.

slides.caption: np.extract() gets the condition [True, False, True, False] and the array [1, 2, 3, 4]. The colours show the condition.
True for 1: kept.
False for 2: dropped.
True for 3: kept.
False for 4: dropped.
np.extract([True, False, True, False], [1, 2, 3, 4]) = [1, 3]

gradient.title: How np.gradient() works
gradient.description: Estimates the slope between neighbouring values.

slides.caption: np.gradient() gets [1, 2, 4, 7, 11]. It estimates how fast the values change at each position.
At the first point it uses the next neighbour: 2 - 1 = 1.0.
In the middle it uses both neighbours: (4 - 1) / 2 = 1.5.
At the last point it uses the previous neighbour: 11 - 7 = 4.0.

interp.title: How np.interp() works
interp.description: Estimates a value between known points with straight lines.

slides.caption: np.interp() gets the point x = 2.5 and known points (1, 10), (2, 20), (3, 30).
2.5 lies between the known x values 2 and 3, exactly halfway (0.5).
So the answer is halfway between their y values 20 and 30: 20 + 0.5 × (30 - 20) = 25.0.

percentile.title: How np.percentile() works
percentile.description: Finds the value below which a given percent of the data lies.

slides.caption: np.percentile() gets the sorted values [10, 20, 30, 40] and q = 25.
The 25th percentile sits at position 0.25 × (4 - 1) = 0.75 along the sorted values.
Position 0.75 is between index 0 (10) and index 1 (20), three quarters of the way: 10 + 0.75 × (20 - 10) = 17.5.

quantile.title: How np.quantile() works
quantile.description: Finds the value below which a given fraction of the data lies.

slides.caption: np.quantile() gets the sorted values [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] and q = 0.25.
The position is 0.25 × (5 - 1) = 1.0 along the sorted values.
Position 1.0 is exactly index 1, so the quantile is 2.0.

trim-zeros.title: How np.trim_zeros() works
trim-zeros.description: Removes zeros from the start and the end of an array.

note.text: only zeros at the ends are removed

slides.caption: np.trim_zeros() gets [0, 0, 1, 2, 0].
The two zeros at the front are cut off.
The zero at the end is cut off.
What is left between the cuts is the result: 1, 2.

kron.title: How np.kron() works
kron.description: Computes the Kronecker product: every value of one array times the whole other array.

note.text: each value of a × the whole of b

slides.caption: np.kron() gets a = [1, 2] and b = [1, 10].
The first value of a, 1, times the whole of b: 1 × [1, 10] = [1, 10].
The next value of a, 2, times the whole of b: 2 × [1, 10] = [2, 20].

hsplit.title: How np.hsplit() works
hsplit.description: Cuts an array into equal parts along its columns.

slides.caption: np.hsplit() gets [1, 2, 3, 4] and 2. For a 1-D array it cuts it into 2 equal parts of 2 items.
It takes the first 2 items and puts them in a new group: [1, 2].
It moves on 2 positions and takes the next 2 items: [3, 4].

meshgrid.title: How np.meshgrid() works
meshgrid.description: Turns coordinate lists into grids of x and y values.

note.text: x = [1, 2, 3], y = [4, 5]  →  two grids of shape (2, 3)

slides.caption: np.meshgrid() gets x = [1, 2, 3] and y = [4, 5]. It builds one grid with an x value in every cell and one with a y value in every cell.
In the X grid every ROW is a copy of x: 1, 2, 3. There is one row for each y value.
In the Y grid every COLUMN is a copy of y: 4, 5. There is one column for each x value.
Cell (row, column) of the two grids together gives a coordinate pair, for example (1, 4) and (3, 5). np.meshgrid([1, 2, 3], [4, 5]) returns [X, Y].

sliding-window-view.title: How np.sliding_window_view() works
sliding-window-view.description: Gives every window of a given length over an array.

note.text: window length 3, moves one step at a time

slides.caption: sliding_window_view() gets [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] and a window length of 3.
The window covers the first 3 values: [1, 2, 3].
It slides one step to the right: [2, 3, 4].
One more step: [3, 4, 5]. The window now touches the end.
The result is a 2-D array with one window per row: [[1, 2, 3], [2, 3, 4], [3, 4, 5]]. It is a view, so no data is copied.

broadcast-shapes.title: How np.broadcast_shapes() works
broadcast-shapes.description: Works out the shape that arrays of different shapes broadcast to.

note.text: compare the shapes from the right

slides.caption: np.broadcast_shapes() gets the shapes (2, 1) and (3,).
The shapes are compared starting from the right: 1 and 3. A length of 1 can be stretched, so the result is 3.
Next axis to the left: only the first shape has one (2). The second has none, so the result is 2.
The broadcast shape is (2, 3).
np.broadcast_shapes((2, 1), (3,)) = (2, 3)

real.title: How np.real() works
real.description: Gives the real part of complex numbers.

note.text: a complex number is real + imaginary·j

slides.caption: np.real() gets two complex numbers.
1+2j has the real part 1.0 and the imaginary part 2.
3+4j has the real part 3.0.

imag.title: How np.imag() works
imag.description: Gives the imaginary part of complex numbers.

note.text: a complex number is real + imaginary·j

slides.caption: np.imag() gets two complex numbers.
1+2j has the imaginary part 2.0.
3+4j has the imaginary part 4.0.

iscomplex.title: How np.iscomplex() works
iscomplex.description: Tests which values have a non-zero imaginary part.

note.text: True if the imaginary part is not zero

slides.caption: np.iscomplex() gets [1+2j, 3].
1+2j has an imaginary part of 2, which is not zero: True.
3 has an imaginary part of 0: False.
np.iscomplex([1+2j, 3]) = [True, False]

nan-to-num.title: How np.nan_to_num() works
nan-to-num.description: Replaces NaN (and infinity) with ordinary numbers.

slides.caption: np.nan_to_num() gets [1.0, nan]. nan means "not a number".
1.0 is a normal number: it stays.
nan is replaced by 0.0.

isposinf.title: How np.isposinf() works
isposinf.description: Tests which values are positive infinity.

slides.caption: np.isposinf() gets [1.0, inf, -inf].
1.0 is an ordinary number: False.
inf is positive infinity: True.
-inf is NEGATIVE infinity: False.
np.isposinf([1.0, inf, -inf]) = [False, True, False]

tri.title: How np.tri() works
tri.description: Makes a matrix with ones on and below the diagonal.

slides.caption: np.tri() gets N = 3, so it makes a square 3 × 3 matrix.
A new array with 3 rows and 3 columns is made.
All cells start as 0.0.
Cells on or below the diagonal are set to 1.0.

vander.title: How np.vander() works
vander.description: Builds a table of powers of the input values (a Vandermonde matrix).

slides.caption: np.vander() gets [1, 2, 3]. Each input value gets one row holding its powers, highest power first.
A 3 × 3 table is made: 3 values, 3 powers each.

setxor1d.title: How np.setxor1d() works
setxor1d.description: Finds the values that are in exactly one of two arrays.

note.text: in one array but not in both

slides.caption: np.setxor1d() gets [1, 2, 3] (first colour) and [3, 4] (second colour).
1 and 2 are only in the first array: kept.
3 is in both arrays: dropped.
4 is only in the second array: kept.

ediff1d.title: How np.ediff1d() works
ediff1d.description: Gives the differences between neighbouring values of a flattened array.

note.text: each value minus the one before it

slides.caption: np.ediff1d() gets [1, 4, 9].

histogram.title: How np.histogram() works
histogram.description: Counts how many values fall into each bin.

slides.caption: np.histogram() gets 6 values and the bin edges [0, 2, 4]: two bins, [0, 2) and [2, 4].
The values 1 and 1 fall in [0, 2): count 2.
The values 2, 3, 3 and 3 fall in [2, 4] (the last bin includes its right edge): count 4.
np.histogram(...) returns the counts [2, 4] and the bin edges [0, 2, 4].

note.text: pad width 1, filled with 0 by default

slides.caption: np.pad() gets [1, 2, 3] and a pad width of 1: one extra value on each side.
A 0 is added in front and another at the end (the default constant mode pads with 0).
The original values sit in the middle.

nansum.title: How np.nansum() works
nansum.description: Adds up the values, ignoring NaN.

slides.caption: np.nansum() gets values that include a nan.
1 is added: 1.
nan is skipped: still 1.
3 is added: 1 + 3 = 4.
np.nansum([1, nan, 3]) = 4.0 (np.sum would give nan)
np.nanmean() gets values that include a nan.
nan is ignored: only 1 and 3 count.
Their average is (1 + 3) / 2 = 2.0.
np.nanmean([1, nan, 3]) = 2.0

nanmax.title: How np.nanmax() works
nanmax.description: Finds the largest value, ignoring NaN.

slides.caption: np.nanmax() gets values that include a nan.
nan is ignored.
The larger of 1 and 3 is 3.0.
np.nanmax([1, nan, 3]) = 3.0

nanmin.title: How np.nanmin() works
nanmin.description: Finds the smallest value, ignoring NaN.

slides.caption: np.nanmin() gets values that include a nan.
nan is ignored.
The smaller of 1 and 3 is 1.0.
np.nanmin([1, nan, 3]) = 1.0
np.nanprod() gets values that include a nan.
nan is treated as 1, so it changes nothing.
np.nanprod([1, nan, 3]) = 3.0

nanargmax.title: How np.nanargmax() works
nanargmax.description: Gives the position of the largest value, ignoring NaN.

slides.caption: np.nanargmax() gets values that include a nan.
nan is ignored.
The largest value, 3, is at index 2.
np.nanargmax([1, nan, 3]) = 2

nanargmin.title: How np.nanargmin() works
nanargmin.description: Gives the position of the smallest value, ignoring NaN.

slides.caption: np.nanargmin() gets values that include a nan.
nan is ignored.
The smallest value, 1, is at index 0.
np.nanargmin([1, nan, 3]) = 0
np.nanvar() gets values that include a nan.
nan is ignored: only 1 and 3 count.
The mean of 1 and 3 is 2. The squared distances are 1 and 1, so the variance is (1 + 1) / 2 = 1.0.
np.nanvar([1, nan, 3]) = 1.0

nancumsum.title: How np.nancumsum() works
nancumsum.description: Gives the running total, treating NaN as zero.

slides.caption: np.nancumsum() gets values that include a nan.
1 → total 1.0.
nan counts as 0: total stays 1.0.

nanmedian.title: How np.nanmedian() works
nanmedian.description: Finds the middle value, ignoring NaN.

slides.caption: np.nanmedian() gets values that include a nan.
nan is ignored. The values left are 1, 3, 5.
The middle one of 1, 3, 5 is 3.0.
np.nanmedian([1, nan, 3, 5]) = 3.0

polyval.title: How np.polyval() works
polyval.description: Evaluates a polynomial at a given x.

slides.caption: np.polyval() gets the coefficients [1, 2, 3], meaning x² + 2x + 3, and x = 2.
Start with the highest coefficient: 1.
Multiply by x and add the next coefficient: 1 × 2 + 2 = 4.
np.polyadd() gets [1, 2] and [3, 4, 5]. The coefficients are lined up from the right, so the shorter one is padded with a 0 (shown first).
x² terms: 0 + 3 = 3.
x terms: 1 + 4 = 5.
constants: 2 + 5 = 7.
np.polysub() gets [3, 4, 5] and [1, 2]. The coefficients are lined up from the right, so the shorter one is padded with a 0.
x² terms: 3 - 0 = 3.
x terms: 4 - 1 = 3.
constants: 5 - 2 = 3.
np.polymul() gets [1, 2] (x + 2) and [1, 3] (x + 3).
x² term: 1 × 1 = 1.
constant: 2 × 3 = 6.
np.polymul([1, 2], [1, 3]) = [1, 5, 6], which is x² + 5x + 6

polyder.title: How np.polyder() works
polyder.description: Gives the derivative of a polynomial.

slides.caption: np.polyder() gets [1, 2, 3], meaning x² + 2x + 3.
x² becomes 2x: the coefficient 1 is multiplied by the power 2.
2x becomes 2: the coefficient 2 is multiplied by the power 1.
The constant 3 disappears.
np.polyder([1, 2, 3]) = [2, 2], which is 2x + 2

polyint.title: How np.polyint() works
polyint.description: Gives the integral of a polynomial.

slides.caption: np.polyint() gets [3, 2, 1], meaning 3x² + 2x + 1.
3x² becomes x³: the coefficient 3 is divided by the new power 3.
2x becomes x²: 2 / 2 = 1.
1 becomes x: 1 / 1 = 1.
The constant of integration is 0 by default.
np.polyint([3, 2, 1]) = [1, 1, 1, 0], which is x³ + x² + x

roots.title: How np.roots() works
roots.description: Finds the roots of a polynomial.

slides.caption: np.roots() gets [1, -3, 2], meaning x² - 3x + 2.
It looks for the x values where the polynomial equals 0. It factors as (x - 2)(x - 1).
x = 2 makes the first factor 0: check 4 - 6 + 2 = 0.
x = 1 makes the second factor 0: check 1 - 3 + 2 = 0.

det.title: How np.det() works
det.description: Computes the determinant of a square matrix.

slides.caption: np.linalg.det() gets the 2 × 2 matrix [[1, 2], [3, 4]].
Multiply the main diagonal: 1 × 4 = 4.
Multiply the other diagonal: 2 × 3 = 6.

inv.title: How np.inv() works
inv.description: Computes the inverse of a square matrix.

slides.caption: np.linalg.inv() gets [[1, 2], [3, 4]]. Its determinant is 1×4 - 2×3 = -2.
The diagonal values swap places: 1 and 4 become 4 and 1.
The other two values change sign: 2 becomes -2 and 3 becomes -3.
Everything is divided by the determinant -2: [[4, -2], [-3, 1]] / -2 = [[-2, 1], [1.5, -0.5]].

solve.title: How np.solve() works
solve.description: Solves a system of linear equations.

slides.caption: np.linalg.solve() gets the matrix [[3, 1], [1, 2]] and [9, 8]. That is the pair of equations 3x + y = 9 and x + 2y = 8.
It finds the one x and y that satisfy both equations: x = 2, y = 3.
Check the first equation: 3×2 + 3 = 9.
Check the second equation: 2 + 2×3 = 8.

norm.title: How np.norm() works
norm.description: Computes the length (norm) of a vector or matrix.

slides.caption: np.linalg.norm() gets the vector [3, 4]. By default it gives the Euclidean length.
Square every value and add: 3² + 4² = 9 + 16 = 25.
Take the square root: √25 = 5.0.
np.linalg.norm([3, 4]) = 5.0

matrix-power.title: How np.matrix_power() works
matrix-power.description: Multiplies a square matrix by itself a number of times.

slides.caption: np.linalg.matrix_power() gets A = [[1, 1], [0, 1]] and the power 3.
A × A = [[1, 2], [0, 1]]: the top right value becomes 1×1 + 1×1 = 2.
A × A × A = [[1, 3], [0, 1]]: the top right value is now 1×1 + 2×1 = 3.

matrix-rank.title: How np.matrix_rank() works
matrix-rank.description: Counts how many rows or columns of a matrix are independent.

slides.caption: np.linalg.matrix_rank() gets [[1, 2], [2, 4]].
The first row is [1, 2].
The second row [2, 4] is just 2 × the first row, so it adds nothing new.
np.linalg.matrix_rank([[1, 2], [2, 4]]) = 1: only one row is independent.

eigvals.title: How np.eigvals() works
eigvals.description: Computes the eigenvalues of a square matrix.

note.text: for a diagonal matrix: the diagonal values

slides.caption: np.linalg.eigvals() gets the diagonal matrix [[2, 0], [0, 3]].
The matrix stretches the x direction by 2 and the y direction by 3. Those stretch factors are the eigenvalues.
For a diagonal matrix they are simply the diagonal values: 2 and 3.

fft.title: How np.fft() works
fft.description: Splits a signal into its frequencies (fast Fourier transform).

slides.caption: np.fft.fft() gets the constant signal [1, 1, 1, 1]. It tells how much of each frequency the signal contains.
Frequency 0 (the average level) adds all values: 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 4.
A signal that never changes has no other frequencies: the remaining results are 0.
np.fft.fft([1, 1, 1, 1]) = [4, 0, 0, 0]. The real results are complex numbers; here the imaginary parts are 0.

ifft.title: How np.ifft() works
ifft.description: Turns frequencies back into a signal (inverse fast Fourier transform).

slides.caption: np.fft.ifft() gets frequency data: 4 at frequency 0 and nothing else.
All the signal is in frequency 0, the constant level. Its size is 4.
That level is shared over the 4 points: 4 / 4 = 1 each.
np.fft.ifft([4, 0, 0, 0]) = [1, 1, 1, 1] (with imaginary parts 0)

rfft.title: How np.rfft() works
rfft.description: The fast Fourier transform for real signals: only the useful half.

slides.caption: np.fft.rfft() gets the real signal [1, 1, 1, 1]. For a real signal the second half of the fft result mirrors the first, so rfft skips it.
Frequency 0: 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 4.
The signal never changes, so the other frequencies are 0. The result has 4 // 2 + 1 = 3 values.
np.fft.rfft([1, 1, 1, 1]) = [4, 0, 0] (4 values in, 3 out)

fftfreq.title: How np.fftfreq() works
fftfreq.description: Gives the frequency that each fft result belongs to.

slides.caption: np.fft.fftfreq() gets n = 4 samples and the sample spacing d = 1.
The first half counts up in steps of 1 / (n × d) = 0.25: 0.0, 0.25.
The second half holds the negative frequencies, starting from -0.5: -0.5, -0.25.

rfftfreq.title: How np.rfftfreq() works
rfftfreq.description: Gives the frequencies that belong to the rfft results.

slides.caption: np.fft.rfftfreq() gets n = 4 samples and the sample spacing d = 1.
The frequencies count up in steps of 1 / (n × d) = 0.25: 0.0, 0.25.
The last one is the highest frequency, 0.5. The result has n // 2 + 1 = 3 values.

fftshift.title: How np.fftshift() works
fftshift.description: Moves the zero frequency to the middle.

note.text: zero in the middle, negatives first

slides.caption: np.fft.fftshift() gets [0, 1, -2, -1]: the order that fft uses, with zero first.
The second half, the negative values -2 and -1, moves to the front.
The first half, 0 and 1, moves to the back. Now zero is in the middle.

note.text: back to the order that fft uses

slides.caption: np.fft.ifftshift() gets [-2, -1, 0, 1], with zero in the middle.
The upper half, 0 and 1, moves to the front.
The negative half, -2 and -1, moves to the back.

clip.title: How np.clip() works
clip.description: Limits every value in an array to a minimum and a maximum.

slides.caption: np.clip() gets the array [1, 5, 9, 12] and the limits 3 and 10.
Each value is checked. 1 is below the minimum 3 and 12 is above the maximum 10 (red). 5 and 9 are inside the range (green).
Values outside the range are replaced by the nearest limit: 1 becomes 3 and 12 becomes 10. Values inside stay the same.

argsort.title: How np.argsort() works
argsort.description: Gives the positions that would sort an array.

note.text: returns the positions (indexes), not the values

slides.caption: np.argsort() gets [30, 10, 20]. Each value sits at an index: 30 at 0, 10 at 1, 20 at 2.
The smallest value is 10 and it sits at index 1, so the result starts with 1.
The next smallest is 20, at index 2.
The largest is 30, at index 0.
np.argsort([30, 10, 20]) = [1, 2, 0]. Reading the original array in this order gives it sorted: 10, 20, 30.

cumsum.title: How np.cumsum() works
cumsum.description: Gives the running total of the values in an array.

slides.caption: np.cumsum() gets [1, 2, 3, 4] and adds the values up as it goes.
The first result is just the first value: 1.
Add the next value to the total so far: 1 + 2 = 3.
Again: 3 + 3 = 6.
And again: 6 + 4 = 10.

reshape.title: How np.reshape() works
reshape.description: Arranges the same values into a new shape.

slides.caption: np.reshape() gets six numbers in a row and the new shape (2, 3): 2 rows and 3 columns.
It fills the first row from the start of the data: 0, 1, 2.
Then it fills the second row with the next values: 3, 4, 5. The values are not changed, only how they are arranged.

sum.title: How np.sum() works
sum.description: Adds up all the values in an array.

slides.caption: np.sum() gets the array [1, 2, 3, 4] and adds all its values.
Start with the first value: the total is 1.
Add the next value: 1 + 2 = 3.
Add the next value: 3 + 3 = 6.
Add the last value: 6 + 4 = 10.
np.sum([1, 2, 3, 4]) = 10 (one number for the whole array)

mean.title: How np.mean() works
mean.description: Gives the average of the values in an array.

note.text: sum divided by how many values

slides.caption: np.mean() gets the array [2, 4, 6, 8].
First it adds up all the values: 2 + 4 + 6 + 8 = 20.
Then it divides by how many values there are (4): 20 / 4 = 5.0.

max.title: How np.max() works
max.description: Finds the largest value in an array.

note.text: keep the biggest value seen so far

slides.caption: np.max() gets the array [3, 9, 2, 7] and looks for the largest value.
The first value, 3, is the biggest so far.
9 is bigger than 3, so 9 is the new biggest.
2 is smaller than 9, so 9 stays.
7 is smaller than 9 too.

argmax.title: How np.argmax() works
argmax.description: Gives the position of the largest value in an array.

note.text: returns the position, not the value

slides.caption: np.argmax() gets [3, 9, 2, 7]. It returns the INDEX of the largest value.
The first value, 3, is the biggest so far, at index 0.
9 is bigger than 3, so the best index becomes 1.
2 is smaller than 9, so the best index stays 1.
7 is smaller than 9 as well.
np.argmax([3, 9, 2, 7]) = 1 (the 9 sits at index 1)

sort.title: How np.sort() works
sort.description: Returns a sorted copy of an array, smallest first.

note.text: returns a sorted COPY, the original is unchanged

slides.caption: np.sort() gets [4, 1, 3, 2].
The smallest value is 1, so it goes first.
The next smallest is 2.
Then 3.
And the largest, 4, goes last.
np.sort([4, 1, 3, 2]) = [1, 2, 3, 4]. The input array is not changed.

flip.title: How np.flip() works
flip.description: Reverses the order of the values in an array.

slides.caption: np.flip() gets [1, 2, 3, 4].
The last value, 4, becomes the first.
The second-to-last value, 3, becomes the second.
Then 2.
And the first value, 1, ends up last.

repeat.title: How np.repeat() works
repeat.description: Repeats each value of an array a number of times.

note.text: each VALUE is repeated 2 times in a row

slides.caption: np.repeat() gets [1, 2, 3] and the number 2.
The first value, 1, is written 2 times: 1, 1.
Then 2 is written 2 times.
Then 3 is written 2 times.

tile.title: How np.tile() works
tile.description: Repeats a whole array again and again.

note.text: the WHOLE array is repeated 2 times

slides.caption: np.tile() gets [1, 2, 3] and the number 2.
The whole array is written once: 1, 2, 3.
Then the whole array is written a second time.
np.tile([1, 2, 3], 2) = [1, 2, 3, 1, 2, 3]. Compare np.repeat, which repeats each value.

diff.title: How np.diff() works
diff.description: Gives the differences between neighbouring values.

note.text: each value minus the one before it

slides.caption: np.diff() gets [1, 4, 9, 16]. The result has one item fewer.
First pair: 4 - 1 = 3.
Next pair: 9 - 4 = 5.
Last pair: 16 - 9 = 7.

unique.title: How np.unique() works
unique.description: Gives the sorted distinct values of an array.

slides.caption: np.unique() gets [3, 1, 2, 3, 1]. Some values appear more than once.
The smallest distinct value is 1. It appears at index 1 and 4, but is kept only once.
Next comes 2 (it appears once).
Then 3, which appears at index 0 and 3, kept once.
np.concatenate() gets two arrays: [1, 2, 3] (blue) and [4, 5, 6] (second colour).
The values of the first array come first.
The values of the second array follow directly after them.

transpose.title: How np.transpose() works
transpose.description: Swaps the rows and columns of an array.

slides.caption: np.transpose() gets a 2 × 3 array: 2 rows and 3 columns.
The first ROW (1, 2, 3) becomes the first COLUMN.
The second row (4, 5, 6) becomes the second column.

stack.title: How np.stack() works
stack.description: Joins arrays along a NEW axis.

note.text: two arrays of shape (3,)  →  one of shape (2, 3)

slides.caption: np.stack() gets two arrays that have the same shape: [1, 2, 3] and [4, 5, 6].
The first array becomes row 0 of a new, taller array.
The second array becomes row 1. stack() adds a new axis, so the result has one more dimension.

ones.title: How np.ones() works
ones.description: Makes a new array filled with ones.

slides.caption: np.ones() gets a shape: (2, 3) means 2 rows and 3 columns.
It makes a new array with that shape: 2 × 3 = 6 cells.
Every cell is set to 1. The default type is float, so the values print as 1.0.

eye.title: How np.eye() works
eye.description: Makes an identity-style matrix: ones on the diagonal, zeros elsewhere.

slides.caption: np.eye() gets N = 3, so it makes a square 3 × 3 matrix.
A new array with 3 rows and 3 columns is made.
All cells start as 0.0.
The diagonal (row 0 col 0, row 1 col 1, row 2 col 2) is set to 1.0.

linspace.title: How np.linspace() works
linspace.description: Makes evenly spaced numbers between a start and a stop.

slides.caption: np.linspace() gets a start of 0, a stop of 1 and num = 5: it must make 5 evenly spaced numbers from 0 to 1.
The first number is the start (0.0) and the last is the stop (1.0).
5 points make 4 gaps, so each step is (1 - 0) / 4 = 0.25.
Stepping 0.25 at a time from the start fills in the points between: 0.25, 0.5 and 0.75.

dot.title: How np.dot() works
dot.description: Multiplies matching items and adds them up (the dot product).

slides.caption: np.dot() gets two 1-D arrays of the same length: [1, 2, 3] and [4, 5, 6].
Items in the same position are multiplied: 1 × 4 = 4, 2 × 5 = 10 and 3 × 6 = 18.
The products are added up: 4 + 10 + 18 = 32.
np.dot([1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]) = 32 (the dot product, a single number)

where.title: How np.where() works
where.description: Picks values from x or y depending on a condition.

note.text: pick from x where True, from y where False

slides.caption: cond = [True, False, True, False], x = [1, 2, 3, 4], y = [10, 20, 30, 40]. np.where() works column by column.
Where cond is True the result takes the value from x: 1 in column 0 and 3 in column 2.
Where cond is False it takes the value from y instead: 20 in column 1 and 40 in column 3.
np.where(cond, x, y) = [1, 20, 3, 40]

argmin.title: How np.argmin() works
argmin.description: Gives the position of the smallest value in an array.

note.text: returns the position, not the value

slides.caption: np.argmin() gets [3, 9, 2, 7]. It returns the INDEX of the smallest value.
The first value, 3, is the smallest so far, at index 0.
9 is not smaller than 3, so the best index stays 0.
2 is smaller than 3, so the best index becomes 2.
7 is not smaller than 2.
np.argmin([3, 9, 2, 7]) = 2 (the 2 sits at index 2)

min.title: How np.min() works
min.description: Finds the smallest value, either in the whole array or along an axis.

slides.caption: np.min() gets a 2 × 2 array. With axis=0 it works on each column separately.
Column 0 holds 3 and 2. The smaller one is 2.
Column 1 holds 9 and 7. The smaller one is 7.
np.min([[3, 9], [2, 7]], axis=0) = [2, 7]. Without axis it would return the one smallest value of everything: 2.

prod.title: How np.prod() works
prod.description: Multiplies all the values in an array.

slides.caption: np.prod() gets [1, 2, 3, 4] and multiplies all its values.
Start with the first value: 1.

cumprod.title: How np.cumprod() works
cumprod.description: Gives the running product of the values in an array.

slides.caption: np.cumprod() gets [1, 2, 3, 4]. Every result is the product of all values so far.
The first result is just the first value: 1.

any.title: How np.any() works
any.description: Tells whether at least one value is true (non-zero).

note.text: True if at least one value is non-zero

slides.caption: np.any() gets [0, 0, 3, 0]. Zero counts as False, every other number counts as True.
0 is False.
0 is False.
3 is True. One true value is enough to make the answer True.
The last 0 does not change the answer.
np.any([0, 0, 3, 0]) = True

all.title: How np.all() works
all.description: Tells whether every value is true (non-zero).

note.text: True only if every value is non-zero

slides.caption: np.all() gets [1, 2, 0, 4]. Zero counts as False, every other number counts as True.
1 is True.
2 is True.
0 is False. One false value is enough to make the answer False.
The last value, 4, cannot fix it.
np.all([1, 2, 0, 4]) = False

var.title: How np.var() works
var.description: Measures how spread out the values are (the variance).

note.text: average squared distance from the mean

slides.caption: np.var() gets 8 values.
Then it squares each value's distance from 5: 9, 1, 1, 1, 0, 0, 4, 16. These add up to 32.
The variance is their average: 32 / 8 = 4.0.

std.title: How np.std() works
std.description: Measures how spread out the values are (the standard deviation).

slides.caption: np.std() gets 8 values.
The variance is the average squared distance from the mean: 32 / 8 = 4.0.
The standard deviation is the square root of the variance: √4.0 = 2.0.

median.title: How np.median() works
median.description: Finds the middle value of an array.

slides.caption: np.median() gets [7, 1, 5, 3, 9].
Sorted, the values are 1, 3, 5, 7, 9.
There are 5 values, so the middle one is the 3rd: 5. The result is a float: 5.0.

average.title: How np.average() works
average.description: Gives the average, optionally giving some values more weight.

slides.caption: np.average() gets [1, 2, 3, 4] and the weights [4, 3, 2, 1]: earlier values count more.
Multiply each value by its weight and add: 1×4 + 2×3 + 3×2 + 4×1 = 20.
Divide by the sum of the weights: 20 / (4+3+2+1) = 20 / 10 = 2.0.

round.title: How np.round() works
round.description: Rounds numbers to a given number of decimals.

slides.caption: np.round() gets [1.26, 2.44, 3.78] and decimals = 1: keep one digit after the point.
1.26: the second decimal is 6, so it rounds up to 1.3.
2.44: the second decimal is 4, so it rounds down to 2.4.
3.78: the second decimal is 8, so it rounds up to 3.8.

count-nonzero.title: How np.count_nonzero() works
count-nonzero.description: Counts the values that are not zero.

note.text: how many values are not zero

slides.caption: np.count_nonzero() gets [0, 1, 0, 2, 3].
0 is zero: not counted. The count is 0.
1 is not zero: count = 1.
0: not counted.
2 is not zero: count = 2.
3 is not zero: count = 3.
np.count_nonzero([0, 1, 0, 2, 3]) = 3

nonzero.title: How np.nonzero() works
nonzero.description: Gives the positions of the values that are not zero.

note.text: returns positions (a tuple holding one array)

slides.caption: np.nonzero() gets [0, 1, 0, 2, 3] and finds where the values are not zero.
1 at index 1 is not zero, so index 1 is kept.
2 at index 3 is not zero: index 3.
3 at index 4 is not zero: index 4.
np.nonzero([0, 1, 0, 2, 3]) = (array([1, 3, 4]),). It is a tuple with one array per dimension.

searchsorted.title: How np.searchsorted() works
searchsorted.description: Finds where a value would fit in a sorted array.

note.text: the array must already be sorted

slides.caption: np.searchsorted() gets the sorted array [1, 3, 5, 7] and the value 4.
1 and 3 are both smaller than 4, so 4 must go after them.
5 is not smaller than 4, so 4 goes just before it: at index 2.
np.searchsorted([1, 3, 5, 7], 4) = 2: inserting 4 at index 2 keeps the array sorted.

take.title: How np.take() works
take.description: Picks values from an array by their index.

slides.caption: np.take() gets [10, 20, 30, 40] and the indices [3, 0].
The first index is 3, so it takes the value at index 3: 40.
The next index is 0: the value 10.

roll.title: How np.roll() works
roll.description: Shifts values along an array; those pushed off one end wrap around.

slides.caption: np.roll() gets [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] and a shift of 2.
Everything moves 2 places to the right. The last two values, 4 and 5, fall off the end and wrap around to the front.
The other values shift right by 2: 1, 2, 3.

compress.title: How np.compress() works
compress.description: Keeps the values where a condition is true.

slides.caption: np.compress() gets the condition [True, False, True, False] and the array [1, 2, 3, 4]. The colours show the condition.
The condition for 1 is True, so 1 is kept.
The condition for 2 is False, so 2 is dropped.
True for 3: kept.
False for 4: dropped.
np.compress([True, False, True, False], [1, 2, 3, 4]) = [1, 3]. This is the same idea as boolean-mask indexing.

append.title: How np.append() works
append.description: Adds values to the end of an array, giving a new array.

slides.caption: np.append() gets the array [1, 2, 3] and the values [4, 5] to add.
The original values are copied first.
The new values follow at the end. The original array is not changed.

insert.title: How np.insert() works
insert.description: Puts a value into an array at a given index, giving a new array.

slides.caption: np.insert() gets [1, 2, 3], the index 1 and the value 99.
Values before index 1 stay where they are: 1.
The new value 99 goes in at index 1.
The values from index 1 on move one place to the right.

delete.title: How np.delete() works
delete.description: Removes the value at a given index, giving a new array.

slides.caption: np.delete() gets [1, 2, 3, 4] and the index 1.
The value at index 0 is kept.
The value at index 1 (the 2) is left out.
The rest is kept and closes the gap.

vstack.title: How np.vstack() works
vstack.description: Stacks arrays on top of each other, as rows.

note.text: vertical stack: one array per row

slides.caption: np.vstack() gets two 1-D arrays of the same length: [1, 2, 3] and [4, 5, 6].
The first array becomes the top row.
The second array becomes the row below it.
np.hstack() gets two 1-D arrays: [1, 2, 3] and [4, 5, 6].
The first array comes first.
The second array is placed right after it. For 1-D arrays this is the same as concatenate.

split.title: How np.split() works
split.description: Cuts an array into equal parts.

slides.caption: np.split() gets [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6] and 3. It must cut the array into 3 equal parts, so each part has 2 items.
It takes the first 2 items and puts them in a new group: [1, 2].
It moves on 2 positions and takes the next 2 items: [3, 4].
It moves on 2 positions and takes the next 2 items: [5, 6].

array-split.title: How np.array_split() works
array-split.description: Cuts an array into parts, even when it does not divide evenly.

slides.caption: np.array_split() gets [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] and 3. 5 items cannot be cut into 3 equal parts, so the first parts get one extra item: sizes 2, 2, 1.
It takes the first 2 items and puts them in a new group: [1, 2].
It moves on 2 positions and takes the next 2 items: [3, 4].
Only 1 item is left, so the last group is shorter: [5]. Then the end is reached.

full.title: How np.full() works
full.description: Makes a new array filled with one value.

slides.caption: np.full() gets a shape (2, 2) and a fill value 7.
It makes a new array with 2 rows and 2 columns: 4 cells.
Every cell is set to 7.

zeros-like.title: How np.zeros_like() works
zeros-like.description: Makes an array of zeros with the same shape as another array.

note.text: same shape and type as the input

slides.caption: np.zeros_like() gets [[1, 2], [3, 4]]. It only looks at its shape (2, 2) and type (integers).
A new array with the same shape, 2 rows and 2 columns, is made.
Every cell is set to 0. The values of the input are not used.
np.identity() gets n = 3, so it makes a square 3 × 3 matrix.
A new array with 3 rows and 3 columns is made.
All cells start as 0.0.
The diagonal is set to 1.0.

diag.title: How np.diag() works
diag.description: Makes a diagonal matrix from a list, or reads the diagonal of a matrix.

slides.caption: np.diag() gets the 1-D array [1, 2, 3]. A 1-D input is placed on the diagonal of a square matrix.
A 3 × 3 matrix is made, one row and column per input value.
All cells start as 0.
The input values go on the diagonal: 1, 2, 3.

outer.title: How np.outer() works
outer.description: Multiplies every value of one array with every value of another.

note.text: every pair: row value × column value

slides.caption: np.outer() gets [1, 2, 3] and [10, 20]. The result has one row per value of the first and one column per value of the second.
A 3 × 2 table is made: 3 values × 2 values.

trace.title: How np.trace() works
trace.description: Adds up the diagonal of a matrix.

slides.caption: np.trace() gets the 2 × 2 matrix [[1, 2], [3, 4]].
The main diagonal runs from the top left to the bottom right: 1 and 4.
It adds them: 1 + 4 = 5.

triu.title: How np.triu() works
triu.description: Keeps the upper triangle of a matrix and zeros the rest.

slides.caption: np.triu() gets a 3 × 3 matrix.
The diagonal and everything above it is kept.
The cells below the diagonal are set to 0.

tril.title: How np.tril() works
tril.description: Keeps the lower triangle of a matrix and zeros the rest.

slides.caption: np.tril() gets a 3 × 3 matrix.
The diagonal and everything below it is kept.
The cells above the diagonal are set to 0.

fliplr.title: How np.fliplr() works
fliplr.description: Mirrors a matrix left to right.

slides.caption: np.fliplr() gets a 2 × 3 matrix. "lr" means left-right.
Row 0 is reversed: 1, 2, 3 becomes 3, 2, 1.
Row 1 is reversed too: 4, 5, 6 becomes 6, 5, 4.

note.text: reverses the order of the rows

slides.caption: np.flipud() gets a 2 × 3 matrix. "ud" means up-down.
The rows swap places: the top row 1, 2, 3 moves to the bottom and the bottom row 4, 5, 6 moves to the top.
Inside each row the order stays the same. Only the order of the rows is reversed.
np.rot90() gets [[1, 2], [3, 4]] and turns it a quarter turn counter-clockwise.
The top row (1, 2) becomes the left column, with 1 at the bottom and 2 at the top. The bottom row (3, 4) becomes the right column, with 3 at the bottom and 4 at the top.
In total, every value moved one quarter turn counter-clockwise around the centre.

ravel.title: How np.ravel() works
ravel.description: Flattens an array into one dimension.

slides.caption: np.ravel() gets a 2 × 3 array.
It reads the first row from left to right: 1, 2, 3.
Then the second row: 4, 5, 6. All values end up in one line.

isin.title: How np.isin() works
isin.description: Tests which values of an array appear in another array.

slides.caption: np.isin() checks every value of [1, 2, 3, 4] against the test values [2, 4].
1 is not in [2, 4]: False.
2 is in [2, 4]: True.
3 is not in [2, 4]: False.
4 is in [2, 4]: True.
np.isin([1, 2, 3, 4], [2, 4]) = [False, True, False, True]

intersect1d.title: How np.intersect1d() works
intersect1d.description: Finds the values that appear in both arrays.

slides.caption: np.intersect1d() gets [1, 2, 3, 4] (first colour) and [3, 4, 5] (second colour).
3 appears in both arrays, so it is in the result.
4 appears in both arrays too. 1, 2 and 5 appear in only one.

union1d.title: How np.union1d() works
union1d.description: Combines two arrays into their sorted distinct values.

note.text: sorted values from either, once each

slides.caption: np.union1d() gets [1, 2, 3] (first colour) and [3, 4] (second colour).
1 is in the result.
2 is in the result.
3 is in both arrays but is kept only once.
4 is in the result.

setdiff1d.title: How np.setdiff1d() works
setdiff1d.description: Finds the values of one array that are not in another.

note.text: in the first array but not in the second

slides.caption: np.setdiff1d() gets [1, 2, 3, 4] (first colour) and [2, 4] (second colour).
1 is not in [2, 4], so it is kept.
2 is in [2, 4], so it is dropped.
3 is not in [2, 4], so it is kept.
4 is in [2, 4], so it is dropped.

copy.title: How np.copy() works
copy.description: Makes an independent copy of an array.

slides.caption: a is the array [1, 2, 3]. np.copy(a) will make a separate array b.
np.copy() allocates new memory and copies the values: b is [1, 2, 3]. b and a are now independent.
Now we set b[0] = 99. Only the copy changes.
After b[0] = 99: b = [99, 2, 3], but a is still [1, 2, 3]. A copy never changes the original (unlike a view).

broadcast-to.title: How np.broadcast_to() works
broadcast-to.description: Stretches an array to a bigger shape without copying data.

slides.caption: np.broadcast_to() gets the 1-D array [1, 2, 3] (shape (3,)) and the target shape (2, 3): 2 rows of 3.
Row 0 of the result is the array itself: 1, 2, 3.
The array is stretched along the new axis: row 1 shows the same 1, 2, 3 again.
No data is copied: the result is a read-only view that reuses the same 3 values for every row. This stretching is called broadcasting.

broadcast-arrays.title: How np.broadcast_arrays() works
broadcast-arrays.description: Stretches arrays of different shapes to one common shape.

slides.caption: The first array is a column [[1], [2]] (shape (2, 1)). The second is a row [10, 20, 30] (shape (3,)). Their shapes differ.
The first array is stretched sideways: its single column is repeated to make 3 columns.
The second array is stretched downwards: its row is repeated to make 2 rows.
Both arrays now have the same shape (2, 3). Operations like a + b use this same stretching.

ndarray.title: How the NumPy array (ndarray) works
ndarray.description: The NumPy array: a grid of values of one type, with a shape.

note.text: an ndarray: a grid of values that all have the same type

slides.caption: np.array() builds an ndarray from nested lists: here 2 rows and 3 columns of numbers.
shape is the length along each axis: 2 rows and 3 columns, so (2, 3).
ndim is the number of axes: 2 (rows and columns).
size is the total number of values: 2 × 3 = 6.
dtype is the one type shared by all values. Whole numbers give an integer type, usually int64.

dtype.title: How the NumPy data type (dtype) works
dtype.description: Every NumPy array has one data type, and you can convert between types.

note.text: dtype: the type shared by all values

slides.caption: np.array([1, 2, 3]) holds whole numbers, so its dtype is an integer type, usually int64.
.astype(float) makes a new array in which every value is converted to a floating-point number.
NumPy also picks a dtype for you: np.array([1, 2.5]) becomes float64, because one value has a decimal part and all values must share one type.
A dtype fixes how much memory each value uses and how it behaves. np.array([1, 2, 3]).astype(float) = [1.0, 2.0, 3.0] (float64).

swapaxes.title: How np.swapaxes() works
swapaxes.description: Swaps two axes of an array.

slides.caption: np.swapaxes() gets a 2 × 3 array and the axes 0 and 1 to swap.
The first ROW (1, 2, 3) becomes the first COLUMN.
The second row (4, 5, 6) becomes the second column.

matrix-transpose.title: How np.matrix_transpose() works
matrix-transpose.description: Swaps the last two axes of an array (the rows and columns of every matrix).

slides.caption: np.matrix_transpose() gets a 2 × 3 matrix. It swaps the last two axes.
The first ROW (1, 2, 3) becomes the first COLUMN.
The second row (4, 5, 6) becomes the second column.

einsum.title: How np.einsum() works
einsum.description: Writes sums of products over axes in a short text formula.

note.text: 'ij->ji': input axes i, j  →  output axes j, i

slides.caption: np.einsum() gets the formula 'ij->ji' and a 2 × 3 array. Letters name the axes: i = rows, j = columns.
The output is written as 'ji': j (columns) comes first. So the first row becomes the first column.
The second row becomes the second column.
np.einsum('ij->ji', ...) = [[1, 4], [2, 5], [3, 6]] (the transpose)

column-stack.title: How np.column_stack() works
column-stack.description: Stacks 1-D arrays as the columns of a 2-D array.

slides.caption: np.column_stack() gets two 1-D arrays: [1, 2, 3] and [4, 5, 6].
The first array becomes the first column.
The second array becomes the second column.
np.squeeze() gets [[1, 2, 3]]: shape (1, 3), one row holding 3 values.
The first axis has length 1: there is only one row. That axis carries no extra information.
squeeze() removes the length-1 axis. The shape becomes (3,).

expand-dims.title: How np.expand_dims() works
expand-dims.description: Adds a new axis of length 1.

slides.caption: np.expand_dims() gets [1, 2, 3] (shape (3,)) and axis 0.
A new axis of length 1 is inserted at position 0, in front of the existing axis.
The values are not changed; the array gets one more dimension. The shape becomes (1, 3).

atleast-2d.title: How np.atleast_2d() works
atleast-2d.description: Makes sure an array has at least 2 dimensions.

slides.caption: np.atleast_2d() gets [1, 2, 3]: a 1-D array of shape (3,).
It has only 1 dimension, but we need at least 2.
A 1-D array becomes one row: the shape changes from (3,) to (1, 3).
np.atleast_2d([1, 2, 3]) = [[1, 2, 3]]. An array that already has 2 or more dimensions is returned as it is.

diagonal.title: How np.diagonal() works
diagonal.description: Reads the diagonal of a matrix.

note.text: main diagonal: top left to bottom right

slides.caption: np.diagonal() gets the 2 × 2 matrix [[1, 2], [3, 4]].
The main diagonal holds the cells where the row number equals the column number: (0, 0) and (1, 1).
Their values 1 and 4 are read out into a 1-D array.

shape.title: How np.shape() works
shape.description: Gives the shape of an array.

slides.caption: np.shape() gets an array with 2 rows and 3 columns.
Axis 0 runs down the rows: there are 2 rows.
Axis 1 runs along the columns: there are 3 columns.

ndim.title: How np.ndim() works
ndim.description: Gives the number of dimensions (axes) of an array.

note.text: how many axes does the array have?

slides.caption: np.ndim() gets a table of numbers with rows and columns.
One axis runs down the rows (axis 0).
Another axis runs along the columns (axis 1).
np.ndim([[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]]) = 2: two axes. A flat list like [1, 2, 3] would give 1.

size.title: How np.size() works
size.description: Gives the total number of values in an array.

slides.caption: np.size() counts all values in the array, whatever its shape.
The first row has 3 values.
The second row has 3 values: 2 rows × 3 columns = 6.

ptp.title: How np.ptp() works
ptp.description: Gives the range of the values: the largest minus the smallest.

slides.caption: np.ptp() gets [3, 9, 2, 7].
The largest value is 9.
The smallest value is 2.
The result is the largest minus the smallest: 9 - 2 = 7.

choose.title: How np.choose() works
choose.description: Builds an array by picking from several choice arrays.

slides.caption: np.choose() gets the index array [0, 1, 0] and two choice arrays. Each index says which choice array to read from.
Index 0 at position 0: take position 0 of choice 0, which is 1.
Index 1 at position 1: take position 1 of choice 1, which is 20.
Index 0 at position 2: take position 2 of choice 0, which is 3.

resize.title: How np.resize() works
resize.description: Makes an array of a new size, repeating values to fill it.

slides.caption: np.resize() gets [1, 2, 3] and the new size 5. 3 values are not enough, so the array is repeated.
The original values come first: 1, 2, 3.
The array starts over to fill the 2 missing places: 1, 2.

cumulative-sum.title: How np.cumulative_sum() works
cumulative-sum.description: Gives the running total of the values in an array.

slides.caption: np.cumulative_sum() gets [1, 2, 3, 4]. Every result is the total of all values so far.
The first result is the first value: 1.

cumulative-prod.title: How np.cumulative_prod() works
cumulative-prod.description: Gives the running product of the values in an array.

slides.caption: np.cumulative_prod() gets [1, 2, 3, 4]. Every result is the product of all values so far.
The first result is the first value: 1.
np.cumulative_prod([1, 2, 3, 4]) = [1, 2, 6, 24]

astype.title: How np.astype() works
astype.description: Converts an array to another data type, giving a new array.

note.text: float → int cuts off the decimals

slides.caption: np.astype() gets a float array and the target type int.
1.9 becomes 1: the part after the point is cut off, not rounded.
2.1 becomes 2.
-3.7 becomes -3: it is cut towards zero.

allclose.title: How np.allclose() works
allclose.description: Tells whether two arrays are equal within a small tolerance.

note.text: are ALL pairs close to each other?
