slides.caption: np.allclose() compares [1.0, 2.0] with [1.0, 2.5] pair by pair.
1.0 and 1.0 are equal, so this pair is close.
2.0 and 2.5 differ by 0.5. That is far more than the tiny default tolerance, so this pair is NOT close.
One pair that is not close is enough: the result is False.

isclose.title: How np.isclose() works
isclose.description: Tests, pair by pair, whether values are equal within a small tolerance.

slides.caption: np.isclose() compares [1.0, 2.0] with [1.0, 2.5] pair by pair.
1.0 and 1.0 are equal: True.
2.0 and 2.5 differ by 0.5, much more than the tiny default tolerance: False.
np.isclose([1.0, 2.0], [1.0, 2.5]) = [True, False]

array-equal.title: How np.array_equal() works
array-equal.description: Tells whether two arrays have the same shape and values.

slides.caption: np.array_equal() compares [1, 2, 3] with [1, 2, 3].
First it checks the shapes: both are (3,). They match.
Then every pair of values is compared: 1 = 1, 2 = 2, 3 = 3.
Nothing differs, so the result is True.
np.array_equal([1, 2, 3], [1, 2, 3]) = True

flatnonzero.title: How np.flatnonzero() works
flatnonzero.description: Gives the positions of non-zero values in the flattened array.

note.text: the array is flattened to [0, 1, 2, 0] first

slides.caption: np.flatnonzero() gets [[0, 1], [2, 0]]. It flattens it to one row: 0, 1, 2, 0.
1 at index 1 is not zero: index 1.
2 at index 2 is not zero: index 2.

cross.title: How np.cross() works
cross.description: Computes the cross product of two 3-D vectors.

slides.caption: np.cross() gets two 3-D vectors a = [1, 0, 0] and b = [0, 1, 0].
np.cross([1, 0, 0], [0, 1, 0]) = [0, 0, 1]: a vector at right angles to both inputs.

convolve.title: How np.convolve() works
convolve.description: Slides one sequence over another, adding up products.

note.text: result[n] = sum of a[k] × v[n - k]

slides.caption: np.convolve() gets a = [1, 2, 3] and v = [0, 1]. The result has 3 + 2 - 1 = 4 values.
np.convolve([1, 2, 3], [0, 1]) = [0, 1, 2, 3]: the input shifted by one place.

full-like.title: How np.full_like() works
full-like.description: Makes an array filled with one value, shaped like another array.

note.text: same shape as the input, filled with 9

slides.caption: np.full_like() gets [1, 2, 3] and the fill value 9. It only uses the shape (3,) of the first array.
A new array with the same shape, 3 cells, is made.
Every cell is set to 9.

ones-like.title: How np.ones_like() works
ones-like.description: Makes an array of ones with the same shape as another array.

note.text: same shape and type as the input

slides.caption: np.ones_like() gets [[1, 2], [3, 4]]. It only looks at its shape (2, 2) and type (integers).
A new array with the same shape, 2 rows and 2 columns, is made.
Every cell is set to 1.

geomspace.title: How np.geomspace() works
geomspace.description: Makes numbers spaced evenly on a multiplication scale.

slides.caption: np.geomspace() gets start 1, stop 1000 and num 4: four numbers where each is the previous one times the same factor.
The first number is the start (1.0) and the last is the stop (1000.0).
4 numbers make 3 steps. The factor is (1000 / 1) ^ (1/3) = 10.
Multiplying by 10 each time fills in the middle: 10.0 and 100.0.

logspace.title: How np.logspace() works
logspace.description: Makes numbers whose exponents are evenly spaced.

slides.caption: np.logspace() gets start exponent 0, stop exponent 3 and num 4.
First it makes 4 evenly spaced exponents from 0 to 3: 0, 1, 2, 3.
Then it raises 10 to each exponent: 10^0 = 1 and 10^1 = 10.

digitize.title: How np.digitize() works
digitize.description: Tells which bin each value falls in.

slides.caption: np.digitize() gets 4 values and the bin edges [0, 1, 2.5, 4, 10]. Bin 1 is [0, 1), bin 2 is [1, 2.5), bin 3 is [2.5, 4), bin 4 is [4, 10).
0.2 lies in [0, 1): bin 1.
6.4 lies in [4, 10): bin 4.
3.0 lies in [2.5, 4): bin 3.
1.6 lies in [1, 2.5): bin 2.

extract.title: How np.extract() works
extract.description: Picks the values where a condition is true.

slides.caption: np.extract() gets the condition [True, False, True, False] and the array [1, 2, 3, 4]. The colours show the condition.
True for 1: kept.
False for 2: dropped.
True for 3: kept.
False for 4: dropped.
np.extract([True, False, True, False], [1, 2, 3, 4]) = [1, 3]

gradient.title: How np.gradient() works
gradient.description: Estimates the slope between neighbouring values.

slides.caption: np.gradient() gets [1, 2, 4, 7, 11]. It estimates how fast the values change at each position.
At the first point it uses the next neighbour: 2 - 1 = 1.0.
In the middle it uses both neighbours: (4 - 1) / 2 = 1.5.
At the last point it uses the previous neighbour: 11 - 7 = 4.0.

interp.title: How np.interp() works
interp.description: Estimates a value between known points with straight lines.

slides.caption: np.interp() gets the point x = 2.5 and known points (1, 10), (2, 20), (3, 30).
2.5 lies between the known x values 2 and 3, exactly halfway (0.5).
So the answer is halfway between their y values 20 and 30: 20 + 0.5 × (30 - 20) = 25.0.

percentile.title: How np.percentile() works
percentile.description: Finds the value below which a given percent of the data lies.

slides.caption: np.percentile() gets the sorted values [10, 20, 30, 40] and q = 25.
The 25th percentile sits at position 0.25 × (4 - 1) = 0.75 along the sorted values.
Position 0.75 is between index 0 (10) and index 1 (20), three quarters of the way: 10 + 0.75 × (20 - 10) = 17.5.

quantile.title: How np.quantile() works
quantile.description: Finds the value below which a given fraction of the data lies.

slides.caption: np.quantile() gets the sorted values [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] and q = 0.25.
The position is 0.25 × (5 - 1) = 1.0 along the sorted values.
Position 1.0 is exactly index 1, so the quantile is 2.0.

trapezoid.title: How np.trapezoid() works
trapezoid.description: Estimates the area under a curve with trapezoids.

slides.caption: np.trapezoid() gets the heights [1, 2, 3], spaced 1 apart.
The first trapezoid has heights 1 and 2: area (1 + 2) / 2 = 1.5.
The second has heights 2 and 3: area (2 + 3) / 2 = 2.5. The total is 1.5 + 2.5 = 4.0.
np.trapezoid([1, 2, 3]) = 4.0

trim-zeros.title: How np.trim_zeros() works
trim-zeros.description: Removes zeros from the start and the end of an array.

note.text: only zeros at the ends are removed

slides.caption: np.trim_zeros() gets [0, 0, 1, 2, 0].
The two zeros at the front are cut off.
The zero at the end is cut off.
What is left between the cuts is the result: 1, 2.

kron.title: How np.kron() works
kron.description: Computes the Kronecker product: every value of one array times the whole other array.

note.text: each value of a × the whole of b

slides.caption: np.kron() gets a = [1, 2] and b = [1, 10].
The first value of a, 1, times the whole of b: 1 × [1, 10] = [1, 10].
The next value of a, 2, times the whole of b: 2 × [1, 10] = [2, 20].

hsplit.title: How np.hsplit() works
hsplit.description: Cuts an array into equal parts along its columns.

slides.caption: np.hsplit() gets [1, 2, 3, 4] and 2. For a 1-D array it cuts it into 2 equal parts of 2 items.
It takes the first 2 items and puts them in a new group: [1, 2].
It moves on 2 positions and takes the next 2 items: [3, 4].

meshgrid.title: How np.meshgrid() works
meshgrid.description: Turns coordinate lists into grids of x and y values.

note.text: x = [1, 2, 3], y = [4, 5]  →  two grids of shape (2, 3)

slides.caption: np.meshgrid() gets x = [1, 2, 3] and y = [4, 5]. It builds one grid with an x value in every cell and one with a y value in every cell.
In the X grid every ROW is a copy of x: 1, 2, 3. There is one row for each y value.
In the Y grid every COLUMN is a copy of y: 4, 5. There is one column for each x value.
Cell (row, column) of the two grids together gives a coordinate pair, for example (1, 4) and (3, 5). np.meshgrid([1, 2, 3], [4, 5]) returns [X, Y].

sliding-window-view.title: How np.sliding_window_view() works
sliding-window-view.description: Gives every window of a given length over an array.

note.text: window length 3, moves one step at a time

slides.caption: sliding_window_view() gets [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] and a window length of 3.
The window covers the first 3 values: [1, 2, 3].
It slides one step to the right: [2, 3, 4].
One more step: [3, 4, 5]. The window now touches the end.
The result is a 2-D array with one window per row: [[1, 2, 3], [2, 3, 4], [3, 4, 5]]. It is a view, so no data is copied.

broadcast-shapes.title: How np.broadcast_shapes() works
broadcast-shapes.description: Works out the shape that arrays of different shapes broadcast to.

note.text: compare the shapes from the right

slides.caption: np.broadcast_shapes() gets the shapes (2, 1) and (3,).
The shapes are compared starting from the right: 1 and 3. A length of 1 can be stretched, so the result is 3.
Next axis to the left: only the first shape has one (2). The second has none, so the result is 2.
The broadcast shape is (2, 3).
np.broadcast_shapes((2, 1), (3,)) = (2, 3)

real.title: How np.real() works
real.description: Gives the real part of complex numbers.

note.text: a complex number is real + imaginary·j

slides.caption: np.real() gets two complex numbers.
1+2j has the real part 1.0 and the imaginary part 2.
3+4j has the real part 3.0.

imag.title: How np.imag() works
imag.description: Gives the imaginary part of complex numbers.

note.text: a complex number is real + imaginary·j

slides.caption: np.imag() gets two complex numbers.
1+2j has the imaginary part 2.0.
3+4j has the imaginary part 4.0.

iscomplex.title: How np.iscomplex() works
iscomplex.description: Tests which values have a non-zero imaginary part.

note.text: True if the imaginary part is not zero

slides.caption: np.iscomplex() gets [1+2j, 3].
1+2j has an imaginary part of 2, which is not zero: True.
3 has an imaginary part of 0: False.
np.iscomplex([1+2j, 3]) = [True, False]

nan-to-num.title: How np.nan_to_num() works
nan-to-num.description: Replaces NaN (and infinity) with ordinary numbers.

slides.caption: np.nan_to_num() gets [1.0, nan]. nan means "not a number".
1.0 is a normal number: it stays.
nan is replaced by 0.0.

isposinf.title: How np.isposinf() works
isposinf.description: Tests which values are positive infinity.

slides.caption: np.isposinf() gets [1.0, inf, -inf].
1.0 is an ordinary number: False.
inf is positive infinity: True.
-inf is NEGATIVE infinity: False.
np.isposinf([1.0, inf, -inf]) = [False, True, False]

tri.title: How np.tri() works
tri.description: Makes a matrix with ones on and below the diagonal.

slides.caption: np.tri() gets N = 3, so it makes a square 3 × 3 matrix.
A new array with 3 rows and 3 columns is made.
All cells start as 0.0.
Cells on or below the diagonal are set to 1.0.

vander.title: How np.vander() works
vander.description: Builds a table of powers of the input values (a Vandermonde matrix).

slides.caption: np.vander() gets [1, 2, 3]. Each input value gets one row holding its powers, highest power first.
A 3 × 3 table is made: 3 values, 3 powers each.

setxor1d.title: How np.setxor1d() works
setxor1d.description: Finds the values that are in exactly one of two arrays.

note.text: in one array but not in both

slides.caption: np.setxor1d() gets [1, 2, 3] (first colour) and [3, 4] (second colour).
1 and 2 are only in the first array: kept.
3 is in both arrays: dropped.
4 is only in the second array: kept.

ediff1d.title: How np.ediff1d() works
ediff1d.description: Gives the differences between neighbouring values of a flattened array.

note.text: each value minus the one before it

slides.caption: np.ediff1d() gets [1, 4, 9].

histogram.title: How np.histogram() works
histogram.description: Counts how many values fall into each bin.

slides.caption: np.histogram() gets 6 values and the bin edges [0, 2, 4]: two bins, [0, 2) and [2, 4].
The values 1 and 1 fall in [0, 2): count 2.
The values 2, 3, 3 and 3 fall in [2, 4] (the last bin includes its right edge): count 4.
np.histogram(...) returns the counts [2, 4] and the bin edges [0, 2, 4].

note.text: pad width 1, filled with 0 by default

slides.caption: np.pad() gets [1, 2, 3] and a pad width of 1: one extra value on each side.
A 0 is added in front and another at the end (the default constant mode pads with 0).
The original values sit in the middle.

nansum.title: How np.nansum() works
nansum.description: Adds up the values, ignoring NaN.

slides.caption: np.nansum() gets values that include a nan.
1 is added: 1.
nan is skipped: still 1.
3 is added: 1 + 3 = 4.
np.nansum([1, nan, 3]) = 4.0 (np.sum would give nan)
np.nanmean() gets values that include a nan.
nan is ignored: only 1 and 3 count.
Their average is (1 + 3) / 2 = 2.0.
np.nanmean([1, nan, 3]) = 2.0

nanmax.title: How np.nanmax() works
nanmax.description: Finds the largest value, ignoring NaN.

slides.caption: np.nanmax() gets values that include a nan.
nan is ignored.
The larger of 1 and 3 is 3.0.
np.nanmax([1, nan, 3]) = 3.0

nanmin.title: How np.nanmin() works
nanmin.description: Finds the smallest value, ignoring NaN.

slides.caption: np.nanmin() gets values that include a nan.
nan is ignored.
The smaller of 1 and 3 is 1.0.
np.nanmin([1, nan, 3]) = 1.0
np.nanprod() gets values that include a nan.
nan is treated as 1, so it changes nothing.
np.nanprod([1, nan, 3]) = 3.0

nanargmax.title: How np.nanargmax() works
nanargmax.description: Gives the position of the largest value, ignoring NaN.

slides.caption: np.nanargmax() gets values that include a nan.
nan is ignored.
The largest value, 3, is at index 2.
np.nanargmax([1, nan, 3]) = 2

nanargmin.title: How np.nanargmin() works
nanargmin.description: Gives the position of the smallest value, ignoring NaN.

slides.caption: np.nanargmin() gets values that include a nan.
nan is ignored.
The smallest value, 1, is at index 0.
np.nanargmin([1, nan, 3]) = 0
np.nanvar() gets values that include a nan.
nan is ignored: only 1 and 3 count.
The mean of 1 and 3 is 2. The squared distances are 1 and 1, so the variance is (1 + 1) / 2 = 1.0.
np.nanvar([1, nan, 3]) = 1.0

nancumsum.title: How np.nancumsum() works
nancumsum.description: Gives the running total, treating NaN as zero.

slides.caption: np.nancumsum() gets values that include a nan.
1 → total 1.0.
nan counts as 0: total stays 1.0.

nanmedian.title: How np.nanmedian() works
nanmedian.description: Finds the middle value, ignoring NaN.

slides.caption: np.nanmedian() gets values that include a nan.
nan is ignored. The values left are 1, 3, 5.
The middle one of 1, 3, 5 is 3.0.
np.nanmedian([1, nan, 3, 5]) = 3.0

polyval.title: How np.polyval() works
polyval.description: Evaluates a polynomial at a given x.

slides.caption: np.polyval() gets the coefficients [1, 2, 3], meaning x² + 2x + 3, and x = 2.
Start with the highest coefficient: 1.
Multiply by x and add the next coefficient: 1 × 2 + 2 = 4.
np.polyadd() gets [1, 2] and [3, 4, 5]. The coefficients are lined up from the right, so the shorter one is padded with a 0 (shown first).
x² terms: 0 + 3 = 3.
x terms: 1 + 4 = 5.
constants: 2 + 5 = 7.
np.polysub() gets [3, 4, 5] and [1, 2]. The coefficients are lined up from the right, so the shorter one is padded with a 0.
x² terms: 3 - 0 = 3.
x terms: 4 - 1 = 3.
constants: 5 - 2 = 3.
np.polymul() gets [1, 2] (x + 2) and [1, 3] (x + 3).
x² term: 1 × 1 = 1.
constant: 2 × 3 = 6.
np.polymul([1, 2], [1, 3]) = [1, 5, 6], which is x² + 5x + 6

polyder.title: How np.polyder() works
polyder.description: Gives the derivative of a polynomial.

slides.caption: np.polyder() gets [1, 2, 3], meaning x² + 2x + 3.
x² becomes 2x: the coefficient 1 is multiplied by the power 2.
2x becomes 2: the coefficient 2 is multiplied by the power 1.
The constant 3 disappears.
np.polyder([1, 2, 3]) = [2, 2], which is 2x + 2

polyint.title: How np.polyint() works
polyint.description: Gives the integral of a polynomial.

slides.caption: np.polyint() gets [3, 2, 1], meaning 3x² + 2x + 1.
3x² becomes x³: the coefficient 3 is divided by the new power 3.
2x becomes x²: 2 / 2 = 1.
1 becomes x: 1 / 1 = 1.
The constant of integration is 0 by default.
np.polyint([3, 2, 1]) = [1, 1, 1, 0], which is x³ + x² + x

roots.title: How np.roots() works
roots.description: Finds the roots of a polynomial.

slides.caption: np.roots() gets [1, -3, 2], meaning x² - 3x + 2.
It looks for the x values where the polynomial equals 0. It factors as (x - 2)(x - 1).
x = 2 makes the first factor 0: check 4 - 6 + 2 = 0.
x = 1 makes the second factor 0: check 1 - 3 + 2 = 0.

det.title: How np.det() works
det.description: Computes the determinant of a square matrix.

slides.caption: np.linalg.det() gets the 2 × 2 matrix [[1, 2], [3, 4]].
Multiply the main diagonal: 1 × 4 = 4.
Multiply the other diagonal: 2 × 3 = 6.

inv.title: How np.inv() works
inv.description: Computes the inverse of a square matrix.

slides.caption: np.linalg.inv() gets [[1, 2], [3, 4]]. Its determinant is 1×4 - 2×3 = -2.
The diagonal values swap places: 1 and 4 become 4 and 1.
The other two values change sign: 2 becomes -2 and 3 becomes -3.
Everything is divided by the determinant -2: [[4, -2], [-3, 1]] / -2 = [[-2, 1], [1.5, -0.5]].

solve.title: How np.solve() works
solve.description: Solves a system of linear equations.

slides.caption: np.linalg.solve() gets the matrix [[3, 1], [1, 2]] and [9, 8]. That is the pair of equations 3x + y = 9 and x + 2y = 8.
It finds the one x and y that satisfy both equations: x = 2, y = 3.
Check the first equation: 3×2 + 3 = 9.
Check the second equation: 2 + 2×3 = 8.

norm.title: How np.norm() works
norm.description: Computes the length (norm) of a vector or matrix.

slides.caption: np.linalg.norm() gets the vector [3, 4]. By default it gives the Euclidean length.
Square every value and add: 3² + 4² = 9 + 16 = 25.
Take the square root: √25 = 5.0.
np.linalg.norm([3, 4]) = 5.0

matrix-power.title: How np.matrix_power() works
matrix-power.description: Multiplies a square matrix by itself a number of times.

slides.caption: np.linalg.matrix_power() gets A = [[1, 1], [0, 1]] and the power 3.
A × A = [[1, 2], [0, 1]]: the top right value becomes 1×1 + 1×1 = 2.
A × A × A = [[1, 3], [0, 1]]: the top right value is now 1×1 + 2×1 = 3.

matrix-rank.title: How np.matrix_rank() works
matrix-rank.description: Counts how many rows or columns of a matrix are independent.

slides.caption: np.linalg.matrix_rank() gets [[1, 2], [2, 4]].
The first row is [1, 2].
The second row [2, 4] is just 2 × the first row, so it adds nothing new.
np.linalg.matrix_rank([[1, 2], [2, 4]]) = 1: only one row is independent.

eigvals.title: How np.eigvals() works
eigvals.description: Computes the eigenvalues of a square matrix.

note.text: for a diagonal matrix: the diagonal values

slides.caption: np.linalg.eigvals() gets the diagonal matrix [[2, 0], [0, 3]].
The matrix stretches the x direction by 2 and the y direction by 3. Those stretch factors are the eigenvalues.
For a diagonal matrix they are simply the diagonal values: 2 and 3.

note.text: row of A · column of B

slides.caption: np.linalg.matmul() multiplies A = [[1, 2], [3, 4]] by B = [[5, 6], [7, 8]].
The result has 2 rows and 2 columns. Each cell is a row of A times a column of B.
Row 0 of A · column 0 of B = 1×5 + 2×7 = 19.
np.linalg.matmul(A, B) = [[19, 22], [43, 50]]

vecdot.title: How np.vecdot() works
vecdot.description: Computes the dot product along the last axis.

slides.caption: np.linalg.vecdot() gets [1, 2, 3] and [4, 5, 6].
Add the products: 4 + 10 + 18 = 32.

fft.title: How np.fft() works
fft.description: Splits a signal into its frequencies (fast Fourier transform).

slides.caption: np.fft.fft() gets the constant signal [1, 1, 1, 1]. It tells how much of each frequency the signal contains.
Frequency 0 (the average level) adds all values: 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 4.
A signal that never changes has no other frequencies: the remaining results are 0.
np.fft.fft([1, 1, 1, 1]) = [4, 0, 0, 0]. The real results are complex numbers; here the imaginary parts are 0.

ifft.title: How np.ifft() works
ifft.description: Turns frequencies back into a signal (inverse fast Fourier transform).

slides.caption: np.fft.ifft() gets frequency data: 4 at frequency 0 and nothing else.
All the signal is in frequency 0, the constant level. Its size is 4.
That level is shared over the 4 points: 4 / 4 = 1 each.
np.fft.ifft([4, 0, 0, 0]) = [1, 1, 1, 1] (with imaginary parts 0)

rfft.title: How np.rfft() works
rfft.description: The fast Fourier transform for real signals: only the useful half.

slides.caption: np.fft.rfft() gets the real signal [1, 1, 1, 1]. For a real signal the second half of the fft result mirrors the first, so rfft skips it.
Frequency 0: 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 4.
The signal never changes, so the other frequencies are 0. The result has 4 // 2 + 1 = 3 values.
np.fft.rfft([1, 1, 1, 1]) = [4, 0, 0] (4 values in, 3 out)

fftfreq.title: How np.fftfreq() works
fftfreq.description: Gives the frequency that each fft result belongs to.

slides.caption: np.fft.fftfreq() gets n = 4 samples and the sample spacing d = 1.
The first half counts up in steps of 1 / (n × d) = 0.25: 0.0, 0.25.
The second half holds the negative frequencies, starting from -0.5: -0.5, -0.25.

rfftfreq.title: How np.rfftfreq() works
rfftfreq.description: Gives the frequencies that belong to the rfft results.

slides.caption: np.fft.rfftfreq() gets n = 4 samples and the sample spacing d = 1.
The frequencies count up in steps of 1 / (n × d) = 0.25: 0.0, 0.25.
The last one is the highest frequency, 0.5. The result has n // 2 + 1 = 3 values.

fftshift.title: How np.fftshift() works
fftshift.description: Moves the zero frequency to the middle.

note.text: zero in the middle, negatives first

slides.caption: np.fft.fftshift() gets [0, 1, -2, -1]: the order that fft uses, with zero first.
The second half, the negative values -2 and -1, moves to the front.
The first half, 0 and 1, moves to the back. Now zero is in the middle.

note.text: back to the order that fft uses

slides.caption: np.fft.ifftshift() gets [-2, -1, 0, 1], with zero in the middle.
The upper half, 0 and 1, moves to the front.
The negative half, -2 and -1, moves to the back.
